According to Ms. Ha, dengue fever prevention and control requires regular coordination between the health sector, local authorities, and the people. If only cases are dealt with when they appear without maintaining environmental hygiene and eliminating mosquito larvae in each household, the risk of the disease continuing to spread remains very high. Information on dengue fever prevention and control is disseminated to each residential area through the public address system. Photo: L.D. In An Khe ward, 817 cases of dengue fever have been recorded. Ms. Nguyen Thi Thuy, Deputy Director of the ward's Health Station, said that one of the current difficulties is the low level of awareness of disease prevention among some residents. Despite regular local awareness campaigns and environmental sanitation efforts, there is still a tendency towards complacency, with a lack of consistent inspection and removal of objects that collect stagnant water around homes. The An Khe Ward Health Station continues to coordinate with neighborhood groups to reach out to each household, especially in areas with a high number of cases, guiding people to identify mosquito breeding grounds and proactively eliminate mosquito larvae and pupae. Strengthen propaganda and mobilize people to proactively clean the environment and eliminate mosquito larvae and pupae. Photo: L.D. In Dien Ban Dong ward, the unpredictable weather with alternating sunshine and rain creates favorable conditions for mosquitoes to breed and develop. Mr. Tran Loc Quang, Director of the ward's Health Station, said that dengue fever is an acute infectious disease caused by the Dengue virus, transmitted through Aedes mosquitoes. The disease typically begins with symptoms such as a sudden high fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, pain behind the eyes, fatigue, loss of appetite, and possibly a rash and nausea. Because the initial symptoms are quite similar to some common illnesses, patients often underestimate the condition and self-treat at home. Facing the risk of an increase in disease outbreaks, the Dien Ban Dong Ward Health Station, in coordination with 27 residential groups, is stepping up propaganda and mobilization efforts to encourage residents to regularly inspect their living areas and address stagnant water spots after rain. You may also like Locals participate in training sessions to learn about measures to prevent and control dengue fever. Photo: L.Đ. Applying digital epidemiological maps to identify risk areas. Dr. Nguyen Dai Vinh, Director of the City's Center for Disease Control (CDC), said that the unit has developed a digital epidemiological map system for online surveillance to improve the effectiveness of monitoring, detecting, and handling high-risk areas. The system allows for the visualization of epidemiological data on maps, tracking the distribution of cases by commune and ward; it also integrates functions for displaying case locations, heat maps, delineating buffer zones for disease control within a 200m radius, analyzing overlapping areas between outbreaks within a 400m radius, and monitoring the progression of the epidemic over time. This provides the health sector with an additional tool to identify high-risk areas, supporting localities in determining priority areas for monitoring and treatment. Alongside the application of technology, the CDC, in coordination with commune and ward health stations and medical facilities, is strengthening regular surveillance to detect cases and outbreaks early; investigating disease vectors to assess mosquito density and larval indices to guide appropriate treatment measures. According to CDC monitoring data, the unit conducted 554 proactive vector surveillance surveys, recorded 85 high-index sites, and organized 165 monitoring sessions on mosquito larva eradication in key areas. These results are used to classify areas into three risk groups, serving as a basis for advising local authorities on organizing disease prevention and control: high-risk areas require mosquito larva and pupa eradication once a week; areas with high mosquito, larva, and pupa indices require eradication every two weeks; and remaining areas maintain eradication once a month. The health sector recommends that people spend 10 to 15 minutes each day checking for and removing stagnant water sources and unnecessary water containers to prevent mosquito breeding grounds. People are pouring water and cleaning household items to prevent the breeding of mosquito larvae. Photo: L.D. Intake, treatment, and disease prevention efforts start from each family. According to Dr. Truong Van Trinh, Deputy Director of the City Health Department, dengue fever is increasing in the area due to several reasons, including the disease's cyclical outbreaks occurring every 3-8 years. Following the outbreak in 2022, the number of cases has shown signs of increasing again. In addition, the erratic weather with alternating rain and hot sunshine creates favorable conditions for mosquitoes to breed, making disease prevention and control efforts more difficult. In response to this situation, the Department of Health established three working groups, comprising department leaders and the city's CDC, to conduct surveys and assessments in various localities in order to promptly direct response measures. The health sector is also inspecting preparations at medical facilities, requiring proactive measures regarding human resources, hospital beds, equipment, and medicines to ensure the reception, admission, and treatment of patients. Healthcare facilities such as Da Nang Hospital, Da Nang Obstetrics and Pediatrics Hospital, Son Tra Regional Health Center, and other units are required to review their treatment capacity and be ready to respond when the number of patients increases. Training on patient classification, diagnosis, treatment, and referral is also required. Recently, Da Nang Obstetrics and Pediatrics Hospital organized a training course on the diagnosis and treatment of dengue fever in children under 6 years old; Da Nang Hospital also provided professional training for medical staff throughout the city on the diagnosis, treatment, and referral of adult patients. The Department of Health directed the CDC to procure additional chemicals and proactively support localities that are lacking or have not yet been able to purchase them, so as not to interrupt the implementation process. Dr. Truong Van Trinh advises that localities need to strengthen environmental sanitation, eliminate mosquito larvae and pupae, and treat stagnant water spots, especially after rain. Each household should proactively check and remove discarded bottles, discarded items, plant pots, and tires that can collect water; tightly cover containers holding household water and regularly change the water in flower vases. People also need to proactively get vaccinated against dengue fever, wear long-sleeved clothing, sleep under mosquito nets, and cooperate with health authorities when spraying chemicals to kill mosquitoes. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Researchers Develop First Dengue Serotype 4 Controlled Human Challenge Model by November 21, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Researchers Develop First Dengue Serotype 4 Controlled Human Challenge Model Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers at the University of Maryland School of Medicine and the Institute of Human Virology have established the first successful human challenge model for dengue virus serotype 4. The experimental clinical model is designed to facilitate and accelerate the evaluation of candidate vaccines and targeted antiviral therapeutics against a viral strain that has historically posed persistent barriers to scientific study. Findings detailing the phase 1 dose optimisation and homologous rechallenge trial were published in The Lancet Microbe. Dengue is a mosquito-borne flavivirus comprising four antigenically distinct serotypes designated DENV-1 through DENV-4. Dengue serotype 4 represents a unique public health and research hurdle because it circulates slowly and unpredictably, frequently with decades elapsing between recognized community outbreaks. Consequently, conventional large-scale field efficacy trials have encountered difficulties assessing vaccine performance, leaving recent phase 3 clinical trials unable to generate reliable efficacy estimates for this specific strain. Conducted in Baltimore between April 2022 and December 2023, the study evaluated healthy adult volunteers to establish viral dynamics and clinical safety parameters. Participants received a single subcutaneous injection containing 95 plaque-forming units of the live challenge virus. Following inoculation, volunteers were closely monitored under strict biosafety and containment precautions to prevent secondary environmental transmission. Participants underwent daily clinical assessments for emergent symptoms and had regular blood collections to measure viral kinetics. To ensure local mosquito populations could not acquire the virus and transmit it within the community, all study participants were accommodated in a local hotel during the window in which active virus remained detectable in their peripheral blood. All 14 enrolled participants subsequently developed detectable viremia alongside mild-to-moderate dengue symptoms. Clinical manifestations followed a consistent presentation across the cohort, with rash and fatigue developing in every participant, followed in frequency by headaches. To map immune mechanisms comprehensively, investigators paired clinical tracking with longitudinal immunological and transcriptomic profiling. After the initial viral challenge, participants mounted robust primary immune defenses characterized by significant antibody responses, marked expansion of antibody-producing cells, and widespread upregulation of antiviral genes. The newly validated platform builds upon previous clinical models previously developed for dengue serotypes 1 and 3, forming part of a broader consortium effort focused on establishing human challenge frameworks for all four circulating serotypes. Although the trial was conducted in a relatively small cohort of healthy adult volunteers and requires further validation, the established model provides a critical clinical foundation for ongoing flavivirus countermeasure research. According to study principal investigator Kirsten E. Lyke, MD, Professor of Medicine at the Center for Vaccine Development and Global Health, the dengue virus ranks among the World Health Organization’s top ten global health threats. Lyke cautioned that a recent outbreak in Florida represents only an initial harbinger of the geographic spread of dengue projected to occur across the United States by 2080. Because medical science currently has no approved antiviral therapy to treat dengue infection, developing preventative vaccines remains critically important for protecting human populations both immediately and over the coming decades. Lyke highlighted that controlled infection models allow investigators to test therapeutics, biologic agents, and vaccines in people so that researchers can focus energy and resources on advancing products with confirmed efficacy. The phase 1 dose optimisation and homologous rechallenge trial was funded by the Military Infectious Disease Research Program and the Medical Technology Enterprise Consortium. The experimental clinical model is designed to facilitate and accelerate the evaluation of candidate vaccines and targeted antiviral therapeutics against a viral strain that has historically posed persistent barriers to scientific study. Findings detailing the phase 1 dose optimisation and homologous rechallenge trial were published in The Lancet Microbe. Dengue is a mosquito-borne flavivirus comprising four antigenically distinct serotypes designated DENV-1 through DENV-4. Dengue serotype 4 represents a unique public health and research hurdle because it circulates slowly and unpredictably, frequently with decades elapsing between recognized community outbreaks. Consequently, conventional large-scale field efficacy trials have encountered difficulties assessing vaccine performance, leaving recent phase 3 clinical trials unable to generate reliable efficacy estimates for this specific strain. Conducted in Baltimore between April 2022 and December 2023, the study evaluated healthy adult volunteers to establish viral dynamics and clinical safety parameters. Participants received a single subcutaneous injection containing 95 plaque-forming units of the live challenge virus. Following inoculation, volunteers were closely monitored under strict biosafety and containment precautions to prevent secondary environmental transmission. Participants underwent daily clinical assessments for emergent symptoms and had regular blood collections to measure viral kinetics. To ensure local mosquito populations could not acquire the virus and transmit it within the community, all study participants were accommodated in a local hotel during the window in which active virus remained detectable in their peripheral blood. All 14 enrolled participants subsequently developed detectable viremia alongside mild-to-moderate dengue symptoms. Clinical manifestations followed a consistent presentation across the cohort, with rash and fatigue developing in every participant, followed in frequency by headaches. To map immune mechanisms comprehensively, investigators paired clinical tracking with longitudinal immunological and transcriptomic profiling. After the initial viral challenge, participants mounted robust primary immune defenses characterized by significant antibody responses, marked expansion of antibody-producing cells, and widespread upregulation of antiviral genes. The newly validated platform builds upon previous clinical models previously developed for dengue serotypes 1 and 3, forming part of a broader consortium effort focused on establishing human challenge frameworks for all four circulating serotypes. Although the trial was conducted in a relatively small cohort of healthy adult volunteers and requires further validation, the established model provides a critical clinical foundation for ongoing flavivirus countermeasure research. According to study principal investigator Kirsten E. Lyke, MD, Professor of Medicine at the Center for Vaccine Development and Global Health, the dengue virus ranks among the World Health Organization’s top ten global health threats. Lyke cautioned that a recent outbreak in Florida represents only an initial harbinger of the geographic spread of dengue projected to occur across the United States by 2080. Because medical science currently has no approved antiviral therapy to treat dengue infection, developing preventative vaccines remains critically important for protecting human populations both immediately and over the coming decades. Lyke highlighted that controlled infection models allow investigators to test therapeutics, biologic agents, and vaccines in people so that researchers can focus energy and resources on advancing products with confirmed efficacy. The phase 1 dose optimisation and homologous rechallenge trial was funded by the Military Infectious Disease Research Program and the Medical Technology Enterprise Consortium. news.content_zh: 据 Bioengineer.org 于 2026 年 11 月 21 日报道,马里兰大学医学院和人类病毒学研究所的研究人员已开发出第一个成功的 登革病毒 血清型 4 人类攻击模型。这项研究于 2022 年 4 月至 2023 年 12 月在巴尔的摩进行,涉及 14 名健康成年志愿者,他们皮下注射了 95 个空斑形成单位的活攻击病毒。所有参与者都出现了可检测到的病毒血症和轻度至中度症状,包括皮疹、疲劳和头痛。该模型旨在克服研究血清型 4(其传播缓慢且不可预测)的挑战,并促进 疫苗 和 抗病毒药物 测试。研究结果发表在《柳叶刀微生物》上,该研究由军事传染病研究计划和医疗技术企业联盟资助。尽管该试验规模较小且需要进一步验证,但它为黄病毒对策研究提供了重要基础。该研究强调了开发预防性 疫苗 的重要性,因为目前尚无批准的 抗病毒药物 治疗登革热感染的疗法。

news.content_title: Florida Dengue Cases Reach 651, Experts Warn About Mosquitoes Breeding in Backyards
news.content: Florida homeowners may have more to worry about than weeds and pests hiding in their gardens. A growing dengue outbreak has brought new attention to the small pools of standing water where disease-carrying mosquitoes can breed, including places people might overlook during routine yard maintenance. According to the latest Florida Department of Health surveillance figures , the state has recorded 651 locally acquired dengue cases across 12 counties in 2026. The outbreak is the largest reported in the continental United States in decades, with infections far exceeding Florida's previous annual record of 199 cases in 2023. The outbreak has been concentrated around Tampa Bay, with Hillsborough County accounting for 487 cases and neighboring Pinellas County reporting 116 as of November 14. Although the latest weekly figures suggest infections may be slowing, Hillsborough County has extended its local state of emergency through November 26. Health experts also warn that official case counts may underestimate the true number of infections. For residents, the concern extends beyond neighborhoods with confirmed cases. The mosquito species responsible for much of dengue transmission can reproduce around ordinary homes, turning flowerpot saucers, clogged gutters, and forgotten outdoor containers into potential breeding sites. Embedded media follows; please allow a moment to load. Unlike mosquitoes associated with large ponds or marshes, Aedes aegypti, a major mosquito species responsible for dengue transmission, is well adapted to living near people. It lays eggs along the inside walls of containers that collect water, making residential properties suitable places for reproduction. Kevin Sukovich, a licensed pest control operator who owns Clermont-based Webenex, told the Clermont Sun that homeowners play an important role in controlling these mosquitoes, even when county crews are spraying public areas. "The county can spray the streets, but this mosquito breeds in a bottle cap of water behind your grill," Sukovich said. "Nobody owns that part. The homeowner does." The CDC recommends inspecting outdoor spaces at least once a week. Birdbaths, buckets, children's toys, discarded tires, and flowerpot saucers should be emptied and scrubbed to remove mosquito eggs. Simply pouring out the water may leave eggs attached to the container. Gardeners should pay particular attention to areas where water collects unnoticed. Rain barrels need tight-fitting covers or fine mesh screens, while gutters should be kept clear so water can drain. Water-holding plants and containers also deserve attention, especially in shaded sections of the yard. Removing breeding sites is an important first step, but it does not eliminate every mosquito already living around a property. According to CDC mosquito-control guidance , adult mosquitoes can shelter in dark, humid locations, including beneath patio furniture and around garages. Targeted insecticide treatments may help control them, although products must be used according to their labels. For water that cannot be drained or covered, the agency recommends appropriately labeled mosquito larvicides. These target immature mosquitoes before they become flying adults. Homeowners should select products intended for the particular location rather than applying pesticides indiscriminately around ornamental plants, wildlife habitats, or water features. Personal protection matters, too. Aedes mosquitoes can bite during daylight hours, meaning gardeners are not necessarily safe just because they avoid going outside at dusk. EPA-registered insect repellents, long sleeves, and well-maintained window screens can reduce exposure while residents work outdoors or relax on patios. Dengue can cause fever, severe headaches, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, and rashes. However, not everyone who becomes infected develops noticeable symptoms. Health experts caution that reported cases may underestimate the outbreak's true extent because some infections cause mild symptoms or no symptoms at all. Reporting delays can also make it difficult to measure the outbreak while cases are being investigated. According to WUSF's November 20 report , Florida recorded 27 additional locally acquired cases during the latest reporting week, down from 100 in the preceding report. Although most people with symptomatic dengue recover, the infection can occasionally progress to severe illness involving bleeding, fluid leakage, or shock. The CDC advises seeking emergency medical care for warning signs such as persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, or unusual bleeding, particularly after a fever begins to subside. There is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue. The CDC recommends rest, adequate fluids, and acetaminophen to help manage fever and pain. People who have or may have dengue should avoid aspirin and ibuprofen because these medications can increase the risk of bleeding. Anyone who suspects they have dengue should contact a healthcare professional for evaluation and guidance. For Florida homeowners, preventing mosquito bites begins with paying attention to the places where mosquitoes reproduce. A forgotten bucket, clogged gutter, or water-filled flowerpot saucer can provide breeding conditions even in an otherwise well-maintained yard. With hundreds of locally acquired dengue infections already reported this year, a weekly inspection of outdoor spaces is a simple precaution worth taking. Removing standing water, maintaining screens, and using appropriate insect repellent can help reduce exposure while residents continue enjoying their gardens. Want more articles like this one? news.content_original: Florida homeowners may have more to worry about than weeds and pests hiding in their gardens. A growing dengue outbreak has brought new attention to the small pools of standing water where disease-carrying mosquitoes can breed, including places people might overlook during routine yard maintenance. According to the latest Florida Department of Health surveillance figures , the state has recorded 651 locally acquired dengue cases across 12 counties in 2026. The outbreak is the largest reported in the continental United States in decades, with infections far exceeding Florida's previous annual record of 199 cases in 2023. The outbreak has been concentrated around Tampa Bay, with Hillsborough County accounting for 487 cases and neighboring Pinellas County reporting 116 as of November 14. Although the latest weekly figures suggest infections may be slowing, Hillsborough County has extended its local state of emergency through November 26. Health experts also warn that official case counts may underestimate the true number of infections. For residents, the concern extends beyond neighborhoods with confirmed cases. The mosquito species responsible for much of dengue transmission can reproduce around ordinary homes, turning flowerpot saucers, clogged gutters, and forgotten outdoor containers into potential breeding sites. Embedded media follows; please allow a moment to load. Unlike mosquitoes associated with large ponds or marshes, Aedes aegypti, a major mosquito species responsible for dengue transmission, is well adapted to living near people. It lays eggs along the inside walls of containers that collect water, making residential properties suitable places for reproduction. Kevin Sukovich, a licensed pest control operator who owns Clermont-based Webenex, told the Clermont Sun that homeowners play an important role in controlling these mosquitoes, even when county crews are spraying public areas. "The county can spray the streets, but this mosquito breeds in a bottle cap of water behind your grill," Sukovich said. "Nobody owns that part. The homeowner does." The CDC recommends inspecting outdoor spaces at least once a week. Birdbaths, buckets, children's toys, discarded tires, and flowerpot saucers should be emptied and scrubbed to remove mosquito eggs. Simply pouring out the water may leave eggs attached to the container. Gardeners should pay particular attention to areas where water collects unnoticed. Rain barrels need tight-fitting covers or fine mesh screens, while gutters should be kept clear so water can drain. Water-holding plants and containers also deserve attention, especially in shaded sections of the yard. Removing breeding sites is an important first step, but it does not eliminate every mosquito already living around a property. According to CDC mosquito-control guidance , adult mosquitoes can shelter in dark, humid locations, including beneath patio furniture and around garages. Targeted insecticide treatments may help control them, although products must be used according to their labels. For water that cannot be drained or covered, the agency recommends appropriately labeled mosquito larvicides. These target immature mosquitoes before they become flying adults. Homeowners should select products intended for the particular location rather than applying pesticides indiscriminately around ornamental plants, wildlife habitats, or water features. Personal protection matters, too. Aedes mosquitoes can bite during daylight hours, meaning gardeners are not necessarily safe just because they avoid going outside at dusk. EPA-registered insect repellents, long sleeves, and well-maintained window screens can reduce exposure while residents work outdoors or relax on patios. Dengue can cause fever, severe headaches, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, and rashes. However, not everyone who becomes infected develops noticeable symptoms. Health experts caution that reported cases may underestimate the outbreak's true extent because some infections cause mild symptoms or no symptoms at all. Reporting delays can also make it difficult to measure the outbreak while cases are being investigated. According to WUSF's November 20 report , Florida recorded 27 additional locally acquired cases during the latest reporting week, down from 100 in the preceding report. Although most people with symptomatic dengue recover, the infection can occasionally progress to severe illness involving bleeding, fluid leakage, or shock. The CDC advises seeking emergency medical care for warning signs such as persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, or unusual bleeding, particularly after a fever begins to subside. There is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue. The CDC recommends rest, adequate fluids, and acetaminophen to help manage fever and pain. People who have or may have dengue should avoid aspirin and ibuprofen because these medications can increase the risk of bleeding. Anyone who suspects they have dengue should contact a healthcare professional for evaluation and guidance. For Florida homeowners, preventing mosquito bites begins with paying attention to the places where mosquitoes reproduce. A forgotten bucket, clogged gutter, or water-filled flowerpot saucer can provide breeding conditions even in an otherwise well-maintained yard. With hundreds of locally acquired dengue infections already reported this year, a weekly inspection of outdoor spaces is a simple precaution worth taking. In an extensive cross-national study published in Tropical Medicine and Health, researchers Suhyun Han and Jong-Hun Kim evaluated whether upstream environmental, hydrological, and viral epidemiological indicators could forecast monthly imported dengue risk in Japan and the Republic of Korea more reliably than models relying strictly on past temporal trends and recurring seasonal curves. By integrating international travel volume, Pacific and Indian Ocean sea surface temperature indices, source-country drought measures, and regional viral serotype dynamics into a multi-algorithm machine learning framework, the investigators established that environmental signals substantially reduce case prediction error and enhance directional accuracy across both nations. Dengue is an acute mosquito-borne viral infection transmitted predominantly by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, with global transmission heavily concentrated across tropical and subtropical environments. Globalization, international mobility, and modern commercial transportation networks have substantially magnified the introduction of dengue virus into temperate, non-endemic settings. Infected travelers frequently return while incubating the pathogen or during an active viremic phase, while commercial trade routes can unintentionally disperse competent mosquito vectors or desiccation-resistant eggs stored in commodities such as used tires. When imported infections enter a region hosting established vector populations during warm seasons, autochthonous transmission can emerge, as demonstrated by the 2014 Tokyo outbreak that resulted in 162 domestically acquired dengue cases. In South Korea and Japan, imported dengue cases continue to be detected annually, exhibiting pronounced seasonal peaks in August in South Korea and September in Japan, mirroring country-specific summer outbound travel patterns to endemic destinations such as Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam. Conventional surveillance and predictive modeling approaches in non-endemic regions often rely on case notification counts reported by source countries or short-term regional data. However, the completeness, timeliness, diagnostic infrastructure, and reporting consistency of dengue surveillance systems vary considerably across endemic nations, introducing substantial reporting uncertainty into downstream forecasting models. To circumvent this vulnerability, the researchers constructed a modeling framework that does not rely on foreign government case notifications, turning instead to objective, large-scale physical and biological indicators. Candidate environmental predictors encompassed sea surface temperature anomalies across the Pacific Ocean, including the Oceanic Niño Index, Niño 3, Niño 3.4, and Niño 4 indices, alongside the Indian Ocean Dipole Mode Index. Atmospheric monsoon indices were integrated through the Western North Pacific, Indian, Australian, South American, and Webster-Yang monsoon indices, while hydrological stress in source nations was captured via the Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index across one-, three-, six-, and twelve-month timescales for the capital cities of Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam. To capture broader viral evolutionary pressures, the team also formulated an indicator of viral serotype dominance persistence, defined as the cumulative number of consecutive years in which a specific dengue virus serotype remained dominant within the Western Pacific Region, derived from World Health Organization surveillance records. The analytical time series incorporated monthly data spanning January 2005 through June 2025. To safeguard model calibration against extreme systemic disruption, the three-year window from January 2020 through December 2022 was excluded from both model development and evaluation due to severe coronavirus disease 2019 travel curbs and abnormal imported case fluctuations. The remaining historical sequence was divided into a 180-month training dataset covering January 2005 to December 2019 and a prospective test evaluation dataset running from January 2023 to June 2025. The core target outcome was formulated by adding a pseudocount of one to monthly imported case counts, dividing by official monthly outbound traveler volumes, and log-transforming the resulting travel-volume-adjusted risk ratio. Predictor lags were systematically identified prior to algorithm training using negative binomial regression models with an offset for log-transformed outbound travel volume. Candidate lag search windows were intentionally constrained to realistic reporting timelines, applying a minimum two-month lag across ocean, atmospheric, and hydrological indices to accommodate data dissemination schedules, while evaluating Pacific ocean temperatures across two- to nine-month intervals and fixing serotype persistence to a six-month lag based on earlier empirical protocols. The variable specification that minimized the Akaike Information Criterion was selected for each factor, culminating in 72 distinct candidate predictor sets per country. These sets combined calendar month and secular year trends with systematically varying blocks of climate, monsoon, drought, and serotype parameters, providing the structural input for four supervised learning algorithms: Elastic Net regression, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting. Model training was conducted exclusively on the 2005-2019 dataset using identical ten-fold cross-validation folds fixed by a constant random seed across all algorithms, evaluating up to 36 prespecified hyperparameter combinations per algorithm. To evaluate whether non-temporal predictors generated genuine forecasting value, the authors established a trend-and-seasonality-only reference model fitted via linear regression using identical cross-validation splits. Once candidate models generated predictions on the log-risk scale, values were exponentiated and multiplied by a Duan smearing factor derived from out-of-fold training residuals to counteract retransformation bias before scaling back to monthly case counts against outbound passenger numbers. In the training phase, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting achieved lower cross-validated root mean squared errors than Elastic Net in both countries and were subsequently assembled as base learners into a stacked ensemble architecture. Evaluating meta-learners across thirty hyperparameter sets demonstrated that an Elastic Net meta-learner minimized cross-validated error compared to a Random Forest meta-learner, securing its selection as the final ensemble engine. When assessed against the held-out test dataset spanning January 2023 to June 2025, the final stacked ensemble substantially outperformed the reference model across all evaluated performance domains. In Japan, the stacked ensemble reduced root mean squared error from 23.875 cases in the reference model down to 7.220 cases, while lowering mean absolute error from 19.779 to 5.577. Concurrently, mean directional accuracy, which tracks the proportion of consecutive months in which predicted and observed counts move in identical directions, increased from 48.276 percent to 65.517 percent, and high-risk discrimination measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve rose from 0.863 to 0.876. In South Korea, root mean squared error fell from 28.812 to 6.313 cases, mean absolute error dropped from 24.078 to 5.113, directional accuracy climbed from 44.828 percent to 65.517 percent, and the discrimination curve expanded from 0.742 to 0.756. Linear calibration slopes in both countries shifted noticeably closer to the ideal value of one, improving from 0.361 to 0.674 in Japan and from 0.218 to 0.736 in South Korea. The study also verified model stability through expanding-window rolling-origin temporal validation across the historical period from 2016 to 2019, where predictor selection and ensemble construction were re-executed using only data available prior to each annual forecast window. In these temporal validation trials, the stacked ensemble maintained the lowest pooled root mean squared error in both nations, dropping from 16.388 to 13.250 in Japan and from 29.430 to 9.505 in South Korea relative to the reference framework. Furthermore, the ensemble attained the highest directional accuracy in Japan at 89.4 percent and tied for top performance in South Korea at 72.3 percent. Inspection of normalized meta-learner coefficients highlighted distinct country-specific weighting architectures: in Japan, all three base learners contributed meaningfully, led by eXtreme Gradient Boosting at 67.2 percent, Support Vector Machine at 18.3 percent, and Random Forest at 14.5 percent. In South Korea, weighting proved highly concentrated, with eXtreme Gradient Boosting accounting for 87.3 percent of meta-learner importance, Support Vector Machine representing 12.7 percent, and Random Forest dropping to zero. Standardized variable importance metrics and block contribution analyses revealed that large-scale Pacific Ocean sea surface temperature indices provided the most robust and consistent predictive signal across both countries. Specifically, the six-month-lagged Oceanic Niño Index ranked highest among non-temporal predictors across all base models in Japan, while the five-month-lagged Niño 3 index consistently led predictor importance in South Korea. Drought conditions in endemic source countries, particularly the Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index for Thailand, also demonstrated prominent predictive utility, ranking among top variables in several base specifications. Conversely, atmospheric monsoon indices and regional serotype persistence provided smaller, less uniform improvements across model permutations. Multiple sensitivity analyses, which explored extending lag windows by one month, utilizing Poisson regression for lag selection, shifting outcome pseudocounts to 0.5, and altering high-risk percentiles from the 75th to the 70th and 80th percentiles, confirmed the consistent retention of Pacific sea surface temperatures and Thailand hydrological indicators without compromising predictive stability. Despite these demonstrable predictive gains, the authors detailed several critical operational and epidemiological limitations. The study was restricted to point predictions without generating probabilistic forecasts or uncertainty intervals, meaning that probabilistic calibration and prediction interval coverage could not be verified. Furthermore, the test period was limited to thirty post-pandemic months, during which international travel was steadily recovering, and lag selection was performed once across the full training dataset rather than being iteratively nested inside cross-validation splits. Data resolution constraints also prevented the identification of localized outbreak clusters, family travel groups, or destination-specific flight volumes, as South Korean destination-specific passenger records were discontinued following the abolition of outbound departure cards in 2006. In addition, using single capital-city grid coordinates as proxies for national drought conditions overlooks broader subnational environmental heterogeneity. To facilitate transparent exploration and scenario testing, the researchers deployed an interactive R Shiny web application, while emphasizing that operational deployment in public health agencies will require automated data feeds, expanded post-pandemic observation windows, and individual-level travel records. This research underscores the importance of incorporating objective environmental indicators to better predict dengue risk in non-endemic regions, where imported infections can spark local transmission cycles.

news.source_body_en: A study published on November 24, 2026, by Bioengineer.org explored how climate and hydrological signals can improve cross-national dengue risk predictions in Japan and South Korea. The research, conducted by Suhyun Han and Jong-Hun Kim, aimed to forecast monthly imported dengue cases more accurately than traditional models that rely on historical trends and seasonal patterns. By integrating factors like international travel volume, sea surface temperatures, drought measures, and viral serotype dynamics into a machine learning framework, the team demonstrated that environmental signals significantly reduce prediction errors and enhance directional accuracy. The study used data from January 2005 to June 2025, excluding the period from January 2020 to December 2022 due to the impact of the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic. The final stacked ensemble model outperformed conventional approaches, with notable improvements in Japan and South Korea. However, the study noted limitations, such as the use of capital-city data to represent national drought conditions, which may not capture subnational environmental diversity. This research underscores the importance of incorporating objective environmental indicators to better predict dengue risk in non-endemic regions, where imported infections can spark local transmission cycles.

news.content_title: Dengue more widespread than previously thought
news.content: Dengue is much more widespread than previously thought, researchers have warned, raising concerns that the threat has been underestimated and resources misallocated. An analysis of global data from 1990 to 2024 found that there were 73.9 million cases of the mosquito-borne disease – 10.6 million more than previously captured. "Collectively these data show that dengue is expanding faster, more consistently and more intensely than previously thought," the authors from institutions in the UK, the US, South Africa and Singapore wrote. Dengue, nicknamed breakbone fever, is spread by the Aedes mosquito and it can cause intense muscle, joint and bone aches. The severe form of the disease can be fatal, and it poses a significant burden on low and middle-income countries. The research, presented at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in Maryland, comes as countries including Bangladesh, Malaysia and Cuba are being hit hard by outbreaks of the disease. The paper , not yet published in a journal, found that global incidence rose 34-fold between 1990 and 2024, an average annual jump of 9.1 per cent. Cases rose most rapidly in regions where the virus has recently emerged – Africa, the Middle East and South Asia – and more slowly in Southeast Asia, where it's been established for decades. Researchers found the missing cases by combing through uncounted sources, like ministry of health PDFs and graphics that never made it into global datasets. They then combined this with modelling, to pull together a single database that tracks 35 years of cases by month, allowing scientists to test new hypotheses. Dengue is spread by the Aedes mosquito - iStockphoto/Pawich Sattalerd "We've addressed the patchy data landscape for dengue," Dr Ahyoung Lim, an epidemiologist and modelling expert at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine and co-author of the paper, told the Telegraph from the Maryland conference. "Previously, we didn't have temporally consistent global dengue statistics. This has been problematic, because consistent data is crucial for answering questions related to the dengue burden, evaluating interventions and even just understanding the drivers of transmission," she added. The paper is currently a preprint – it's undergoing the peer-review process, having been accepted by a journal. But Prof Ooi Eng Eong, a professor in emerging infectious diseases at Duke NUS in Singapore but not involved in the study, said it will "form a focal reference point on the global dengue burden". "Underestimation of the annual incidence of cases... undermines disease control efforts," he told the Telegraph . "Providing a number to the growth of the problem is one of the key steps towards appropriate allocation of resources to prevent dengue." Dr Lim said the study doesn't account for under-reporting of dengue – for instance, mild and asymptomatic cases can be missed if people don't go to see a doctor, while some hospital systems are disconnected. This has been a major issue in Bangladesh, where health workers also battling a deadly outbreak of measles are under huge strain. A municipal worker fumigates a market area during a dengue prevention campaign in Colombo - AFP via Getty Images/ISHARA S. KODIKARA So far this year 168,933 people have been hospitalised with dengue and 510 have died in the country, according to the ministry of health – surpassing 2024 and 2025, which both saw roughly 100,000 infections, but still well below the record of 320,000 cases and 1,700 deaths in 2023. But patchy reporting means the real total is "10 times higher", said Prof Kabirul Bashar, a medical entomologist at Jahangirnagar University in Bangladesh and member of the World Health Organization (WHO)'s southeast Asia dengue advisory group. "We have more than 7,000 hospitals and small clinics, but [many do not] report their dengue cases to the government's health emergency centre. Many dengue cases are treated at home, so are not counted by anyone," he told The Telegraph. The virus is thriving in the South Asian country because of a combination of warming temperatures , rapid unplanned urbanisation, and patchy vector control measures – and although the dengue-carrying Aedes mosquito is traditionally a city-dweller, it is now spreading across rural regions. "We've failed at vector control, and now the Aedes mosquito is breeding across the country," Prof Bashar said. "It's becoming a bigger and bigger problem. "In Bangladesh in November and December, dengue cases are usually very low, but now we're forecasting a historical [high]... Dengue has taken over the whole country, not only the city but also the rural areas." New hope As countries across the world battle to control mosquito populations, one of the more promising tools to combat the insects has been Wolbachia . Wolbachia, a naturally occurring bacteria, is found in a range of insects, though not the Aedes mosquito. But when the mosquito is infected with the bacteria, it inhibits the dengue virus's ability to replicate. In effect, the bacteria and the virus are competing for resources – and Wolbachia comes out on top. Countries from Columbia to Laos have released mosquitoes infected with the bacteria – when these insects mate, they pass the Wolbachia onto their offspring. The aim is that, after several generations, the majority of insects in any given area carry the bacteria, which then helps to suppress the spread of disease. On Saturday, also at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, researchers said the Wolbachia method had reduced dengue infections among children by 69 per cent in Brazil – and reduced chikungunya, which is spread by the same mosquitoes, by 73 per cent. The four-year randomised control trial , which has not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal, included 5,750 schoolchildren aged six to 11 in areas with and without Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes. Researchers analysed blood samples to compare infection rates. "These results provide powerful new evidence that Wolbachia can reduce dengue transmission, even during major epidemics," said Dr Luciano Moreira, a special advisor to the World Mosquito Program, which led the work. He added that it builds on previous research. A randomised control trial published in 2020 in Indonesia found dengue cases dropped by 77 per cent in areas of Yogyakarta city where Wolbachia mosquitoes were released, while results in 2023 showed incidence fell by at least 94 per cent in three Colombian cities. Experts hope that interventions like this, along with new dengue vaccines , could eventually help turn the tide against a disease that's been described as a rising global threat. Bangladesh isn't the only place to have a major dengue outbreak this year: government data shows that nearby Sri Lanka has seen 110,431 cases and 82 deaths , with peak transmission was in July, while Malaysia reported 79,600 infections by the end of last month – far surpassing the 55,399 recorded in 2025. Meanwhile in Cuba, the Global Dengue Observatory estimated there were 15,859 cases through October – 10.6 times higher than the expected level. Fuel shortages, blackouts and shortages of basic medicines have affected all aspects of the response. And in neighbouring Florida, an 80-year-old woman called Gay Small died in September as the virus gains a new foothold in the state – there have been at least 252 locally acquired cases this year. "I think the [new figures] are both a warning and a wake-up call," said Dr Lim. "Malaria is also a mosquito-borne disease and shares many things in common with dengue... but they are seeing opposite trajectories. Malaria has seen a decline over past decades, but dengue is emerging rapidly. So we do need more focus on it." news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Dengue Climate Research Aligns With Current Burden but Not Long-Term Trends by November 23, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Dengue Climate Research Aligns With Current Burden but Not Long-Term Trends Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Scientific research examining the convergence of dengue fever and extreme weather has expanded substantially across the globe, yet national publication outputs correspond only modestly with contemporary disease burden and fail to reflect long-term increases in incidence rates. A comprehensive bibliometric investigation evaluating global literature published between 2008 and May 2026 demonstrated that while academic investigations into meteorological drivers of dengue transmission grew markedly after 2020, research productivity remains heavily concentrated within a small cluster of well-resourced nations. Led by investigator teams examining records indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection, the analysis evaluated how country-level research outputs correspond to real-world epidemiological burdens drawn from the Global Burden of Disease 2023 dataset and mechanistic indicators of climate-driven vector suitability. The resulting findings establish that while global investigative efforts are positively associated with current disease metrics, substantial geographic mismatches persist, leaving several nations with extensive transmission suitability and severe public health burdens entirely unrepresented in internationally indexed scientific publications. Dengue fever represents one of the most rapidly spreading mosquito-borne viral infections worldwide, posing acute public health threats throughout tropical and subtropical regions. Primarily transmitted to humans by the vector species Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, the virus has expanded across expanding ecological ranges influenced by urbanization, human population mobility, and environmental shifts. Global health monitoring reported that by late April 2024, more than 7.6 million dengue cases were documented worldwide within a single four-month period, encompassing roughly 3.4 million laboratory-confirmed cases, over 16,000 severe clinical presentations, and upwards of 3,000 fatalities, with active transmission recorded across 90 countries and territories. In parallel, climate change has been identified as a critical driver altering viral transmission dynamics, with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change affirming with high confidence that meteorological variables including ambient temperature, precipitation regimes, relative humidity, and extreme weather phenomena exert powerful regulatory influences on disease ecology. The underlying biological mechanisms linking weather extremes to dengue transmission operate through both direct vector physiology and broader environmental disruptions. Elevated ambient temperatures accelerate the metabolic processes of vector mosquitoes, shortening the extrinsic incubation period required for viral replication inside the mosquito, while simultaneously increasing biting frequency and expanding geographic regions environmentally capable of sustaining vector populations. Conversely, extreme hydrometeorological events, including prolonged heatwaves, heavy rainfall, typhoons, flooding, and droughts, disrupt mosquito breeding habitats and shift human exposure patterns in complex, nonlinear manners. Large-scale periodic climatic oscillations, such as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, further introduce temporal and interannual variations in viral incidence across entire continents. Discover more Check Symptoms Track Weather Check Forecasts Find Treatments Track Outbreaks To rigorously characterize how the global scientific community has investigated these complex interactions, researchers executed a standardized bibliometric query across the Web of Science Core Collection on May 22, 2026. Restricting the evaluation to English-language research articles and reviews published between 2008 and 2026, the systematic screening pipeline identified 796 initial candidate records. Following the exclusion of non-English records, non-peer-reviewed document types such as conference abstracts, book chapters, and editorial notes, and 460 publications that lacked direct substantive links between dengue transmission and meteorological exposures, a finalized corpus of 290 publications was isolated for detailed quantitative synthesis. Analytical processing was carried out using Microsoft Excel 2024, VOSviewer version 1.6.20, CiteSpace version 6.4.2, and the bibliometrix package within R version 4.5.2 to trace annual publication growth, institutional collaboration structures, author co-citation networks, keyword co-occurrence groupings, and journal citation pathways. Annual research production over the eighteen-year evaluation period exhibited a steady upward trajectory characterized by distinct expansion phases. Between 2008 and 2012, annual output remained comparatively low, ranging between 5 and 12 publications per year, before expanding to 13 papers in 2013 and climbing to 22 by 2019. The post-2020 period sustained heightened productivity, reaching 24 publications in 2022 and achieving an annual peak of 28 publications in 2025. Because the database query terminated on May 22, 2026, the final year reflected an incomplete reporting window rather than an actual drop in investigational activity. Across the entire 290-article corpus, participating author affiliations encompassed 66 countries and generated 551 distinct country-publication combinations under a full-counting paradigm, wherein every nation contributing to a multi-author paper received a single publication credit. Discover more Read Med Journals Donate to Research Find Conferences Geographic analysis revealed that international research productivity in dengue and extreme weather is concentrated within a very small set of countries with advanced research infrastructures. The United States contributed to 113 publications, representing 39.0 percent of the total literature corpus, followed by China with 54 publications or 18.6 percent, the United Kingdom with 47 publications accounting for 16.2 percent, Australia with 38 publications representing 13.1 percent, and Brazil with 25 publications or 8.6 percent. International co-authorship networks demonstrated that the United States served as a central collaborative hub, linking research teams across China, Australia, the United Kingdom, Brazil, and several partner institutions in Europe and Asia. However, despite these major international links, dozens of dengue-endemic territories with lower absolute research outputs maintained sparse collaborative connections or remained completely absent from global collaboration graphs. Institutional and financial support analyses reinforced this observed structural concentration. The University of London led global academic output with 33 institutional contributions, followed closely by the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine with 30 contributions, the Pennsylvania Commonwealth System of Higher Education with 26, Pennsylvania State University with 25, and the National University of Singapore with 24. Funding agency acknowledgments, recorded across 222 of the 290 publications, demonstrated that US federal entities were the leading sponsors of indexed research: the National Institutes of Health was acknowledged in 25 publications, representing 11.3 percent of funded works, followed by the National Science Foundation in 19 papers, the National Natural Science Foundation of China in 18 papers, the UK Medical Research Council in 16 papers, and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in 9 papers. These reporting frequencies illustrate national investment profiles, although acknowledgment tallies do not quantify monetary allocations or prove that grant receipt directly caused elevated publication productivity. To evaluate whether research activity aligned with public health needs, investigators linked country-level publication counts with epidemiological indicators from the Global Burden of Disease 2023 study across 80 nations operationally defined as dengue-endemic based on the CDC Yellow Book criteria. Statistical evaluations utilizing Spearman rank correlations demonstrated modest but statistically significant positive associations between national publication volume and contemporary disease burden, yielding a coefficient of rho equals 0.32 (P = 0.004, n = 80) for the 2023 age-standardized incidence rate and rho equals 0.36 (P < 0.001, n = 80) for the 2023 age-standardized disability-adjusted life-year rate. Sensitivity testing confirming these results across the lower and upper bounds of the 95 percent uncertainty intervals for disability-adjusted life-year estimates yielded consistent positive correlations of rho equals 0.40 (P < 0.001) and rho equals 0.31 (P = 0.005), respectively, verifying that the positive alignment with current burden was robust to modeling uncertainty. A critical divergence emerged, however, when researchers evaluated the relationship between national scientific productivity and the long-term trajectory of disease spread. The association between country publication output and the estimated annual percentage change in age-standardized incidence rates between 1990 and 2023 was weak and failed to achieve statistical significance, exhibiting a Spearman rank correlation coefficient of rho equals 0.20 (P = 0.070, n = 80). This finding demonstrates that countries experiencing the most rapid multi-decade accelerations in dengue transmission have not received proportionally expanded scientific attention. National publication volume was more closely aligned with the contemporary level of dengue burden than with its long-term temporal trend. The study further incorporated index-P, a mechanistic indicator derived from microclimatic temperature and humidity variables that quantifies the environmental suitability of local conditions for mosquito-borne viral transmission. When evaluating 63 dengue-endemic nations possessing complete reporting data across disability-adjusted life-year rates, mean index-P values from 1990 to 2022, and Web of Science publication tallies, substantial geographic disparities became evident without constructing artificial composite scores. Several dengue-endemic countries combined relatively high disability-adjusted life-year rates and high long-term climatic suitability with few or no eligible Web of Science-indexed publications. Because index-P captures climate-driven suitability rather than observed transmission—which depends on vector presence, human mobility, and healthcare infrastructure—the researchers emphasized that these descriptive comparisons highlight regional under-representation rather than definitive proof that local scientific investigations were absent. Disciplinary and thematic mapping confirmed that the intellectual foundation of dengue and extreme weather research has evolved from isolated meteorological observations into an integrated, interdisciplinary framework. Lead publishing venues included PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases with 28 articles, the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health and Parasites and Vectors with 14 papers each, Acta Tropica with 11, and the Journal of Medical Entomology and Scientific Reports with 9 each. Co-citation analyses and dual-map overlays demonstrated that citing journals rooted in clinical medicine and molecular biology draw heavily upon foundational cited literature in environmental sciences, nursing, and general public health. Author networks led by Rachel Lowe with 11 publications and frequently co-cited scholars including Simon Hales with 102 co-citations established that early keyword foci on rainfall, temperature, and localized time-series analysis have increasingly shifted toward predictive transmission modeling, urbanization risks, hydrometeorological hazards, and climate-informed early warning systems. The authors outlined essential constraints inherent to their bibliometric methodology. Restricting the literature search strictly to English-language articles and reviews indexed within the Web of Science Core Collection omitted relevant investigations published in regional databases, non-indexed journals, languages other than English, surveillance reports, or grey literature, which may have disproportionately excluded locally published research and underestimated the contributions of some dengue-endemic countries. Furthermore, publication counts were not normalized against national population sizes or total national research expenditures, and bibliometric metrics reflect publication frequency rather than study quality or causal validity. Despite these limitations, the evidence underscores that while scientific attention toward dengue and extreme weather is expanding, international partnerships, surveillance infrastructure, and local research investments must be directed toward under-represented endemic settings facing high climatic suitability and rapidly escalating epidemiological burdens. A comprehensive bibliometric investigation evaluating global literature published between 2008 and May 2026 demonstrated that while academic investigations into meteorological drivers of dengue transmission grew markedly after 2020, research productivity remains heavily concentrated within a small cluster of well-resourced nations. Led by investigator teams examining records indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection, the analysis evaluated how country-level research outputs correspond to real-world epidemiological burdens drawn from the Global Burden of Disease 2023 dataset and mechanistic indicators of climate-driven vector suitability. The resulting findings establish that while global investigative efforts are positively associated with current disease metrics, substantial geographic mismatches persist, leaving several nations with extensive transmission suitability and severe public health burdens entirely unrepresented in internationally indexed scientific publications. Dengue fever represents one of the most rapidly spreading mosquito-borne viral infections worldwide, posing acute public health threats throughout tropical and subtropical regions. Primarily transmitted to humans by the vector species Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, the virus has expanded across expanding ecological ranges influenced by urbanization, human population mobility, and environmental shifts. Global health monitoring reported that by late April 2024, more than 7.6 million dengue cases were documented worldwide within a single four-month period, encompassing roughly 3.4 million laboratory-confirmed cases, over 16,000 severe clinical presentations, and upwards of 3,000 fatalities, with active transmission recorded across 90 countries and territories. In parallel, climate change has been identified as a critical driver altering viral transmission dynamics, with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change affirming with high confidence that meteorological variables including ambient temperature, precipitation regimes, relative humidity, and extreme weather phenomena exert powerful regulatory influences on disease ecology. The underlying biological mechanisms linking weather extremes to dengue transmission operate through both direct vector physiology and broader environmental disruptions. Elevated ambient temperatures accelerate the metabolic processes of vector mosquitoes, shortening the extrinsic incubation period required for viral replication inside the mosquito, while simultaneously increasing biting frequency and expanding geographic regions environmentally capable of sustaining vector populations. Conversely, extreme hydrometeorological events, including prolonged heatwaves, heavy rainfall, typhoons, flooding, and droughts, disrupt mosquito breeding habitats and shift human exposure patterns in complex, nonlinear manners. Large-scale periodic climatic oscillations, such as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, further introduce temporal and interannual variations in viral incidence across entire continents. Discover more Check Symptoms Track Weather Check Forecasts Find Treatments Track Outbreaks To rigorously characterize how the global scientific community has investigated these complex interactions, researchers executed a standardized bibliometric query across the Web of Science Core Collection on May 22, 2026. Restricting the evaluation to English-language research articles and reviews published between 2008 and 2026, the systematic screening pipeline identified 796 initial candidate records. Following the exclusion of non-English records, non-peer-reviewed document types such as conference abstracts, book chapters, and editorial notes, and 460 publications that lacked direct substantive links between dengue transmission and meteorological exposures, a finalized corpus of 290 publications was isolated for detailed quantitative synthesis. Analytical processing was carried out using Microsoft Excel 2024, VOSviewer version 1.6.20, CiteSpace version 6.4.2, and the bibliometrix package within R version 4.5.2 to trace annual publication growth, institutional collaboration structures, author co-citation networks, keyword co-occurrence groupings, and journal citation pathways. Annual research production over the eighteen-year evaluation period exhibited a steady upward trajectory characterized by distinct expansion phases. Between 2008 and 2012, annual output remained comparatively low, ranging between 5 and 12 publications per year, before expanding to 13 papers in 2013 and climbing to 22 by 2019. The post-2020 period sustained heightened productivity, reaching 24 publications in 2022 and achieving an annual peak of 28 publications in 2025. Because the database query terminated on May 22, 2026, the final year reflected an incomplete reporting window rather than an actual drop in investigational activity. Across the entire 290-article corpus, participating author affiliations encompassed 66 countries and generated 551 distinct country-publication combinations under a full-counting paradigm, wherein every nation contributing to a multi-author paper received a single publication credit. Discover more Read Med Journals Donate to Research Find Conferences Geographic analysis revealed that international research productivity in dengue and extreme weather is concentrated within a very small set of countries with advanced research infrastructures. The United States contributed to 113 publications, representing 39.0 percent of the total literature corpus, followed by China with 54 publications or 18.6 percent, the United Kingdom with 47 publications accounting for 16.2 percent, Australia with 38 publications representing 13.1 percent, and Brazil with 25 publications or 8.6 percent. International co-authorship networks demonstrated that the United States served as a central collaborative hub, linking research teams across China, Australia, the United Kingdom, Brazil, and several partner institutions in Europe and Asia. However, despite these major international links, dozens of dengue-endemic territories with lower absolute research outputs maintained sparse collaborative connections or remained completely absent from global collaboration graphs. Institutional and financial support analyses reinforced this observed structural concentration. The University of London led global academic output with 33 institutional contributions, followed closely by the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine with 30 contributions, the Pennsylvania Commonwealth System of Higher Education with 26, Pennsylvania State University with 25, and the National University of Singapore with 24. Funding agency acknowledgments, recorded across 222 of the 290 publications, demonstrated that US federal entities were the leading sponsors of indexed research: the National Institutes of Health was acknowledged in 25 publications, representing 11.3 percent of funded works, followed by the National Science Foundation in 19 papers, the National Natural Science Foundation of China in 18 papers, the UK Medical Research Council in 16 papers, and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in 9 papers. These reporting frequencies illustrate national investment profiles, although acknowledgment tallies do not quantify monetary allocations or prove that grant receipt directly caused elevated publication productivity. To evaluate whether research activity aligned with public health needs, investigators linked country-level publication counts with epidemiological indicators from the Global Burden of Disease 2023 study across 80 nations operationally defined as dengue-endemic based on the CDC Yellow Book criteria. Statistical evaluations utilizing Spearman rank correlations demonstrated modest but statistically significant positive associations between national publication volume and contemporary disease burden, yielding a coefficient of rho equals 0.32 (P = 0.004, n = 80) for the 2023 age-standardized incidence rate and rho equals 0.36 (P < 0.001, n = 80) for the 2023 age-standardized disability-adjusted life-year rate. Sensitivity testing confirming these results across the lower and upper bounds of the 95 percent uncertainty intervals for disability-adjusted life-year estimates yielded consistent positive correlations of rho equals 0.40 (P < 0.001) and rho equals 0.31 (P = 0.005), respectively, verifying that the positive alignment with current burden was robust to modeling uncertainty. A critical divergence emerged, however, when researchers evaluated the relationship between national scientific productivity and the long-term trajectory of disease spread. The association between country publication output and the estimated annual percentage change in age-standardized incidence rates between 1990 and 2023 was weak and failed to achieve statistical significance, exhibiting a Spearman rank correlation coefficient of rho equals 0.20 (P = 0.070, n = 80). This finding demonstrates that countries experiencing the most rapid multi-decade accelerations in dengue transmission have not received proportionally expanded scientific attention. National publication volume was more closely aligned with the contemporary level of dengue burden than with its long-term temporal trend. The study further incorporated index-P, a mechanistic indicator derived from microclimatic temperature and humidity variables that quantifies the environmental suitability of local conditions for mosquito-borne viral transmission. When evaluating 63 dengue-endemic nations possessing complete reporting data across disability-adjusted life-year rates, mean index-P values from 1990 to 2022, and Web of Science publication tallies, substantial geographic disparities became evident without constructing artificial composite scores. Several dengue-endemic countries combined relatively high disability-adjusted life-year rates and high long-term climatic suitability with few or no eligible Web of Science-indexed publications. Because index-P captures climate-driven suitability rather than observed transmission—which depends on vector presence, human mobility, and healthcare infrastructure—the researchers emphasized that these descriptive comparisons highlight regional under-representation rather than definitive proof that local scientific investigations were absent. Disciplinary and thematic mapping confirmed that the intellectual foundation of dengue and extreme weather research has evolved from isolated meteorological observations into an integrated, interdisciplinary framework. Lead publishing venues included PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases with 28 articles, the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health and Parasites and Vectors with 14 papers each, Acta Tropica with 11, and the Journal of Medical Entomology and Scientific Reports with 9 each. Co-citation analyses and dual-map overlays demonstrated that citing journals rooted in clinical medicine and molecular biology draw heavily upon foundational cited literature in environmental sciences, nursing, and general public health. Author networks led by Rachel Lowe with 11 publications and frequently co-cited scholars including Simon Hales with 102 co-citations established that early keyword foci on rainfall, temperature, and localized time-series analysis have increasingly shifted toward predictive transmission modeling, urbanization risks, hydrometeorological hazards, and climate-informed early warning systems. The authors outlined essential constraints inherent to their bibliometric methodology. Restricting the literature search strictly to English-language articles and reviews indexed within the Web of Science Core Collection omitted relevant investigations published in regional databases, non-indexed journals, languages other than English, surveillance reports, or grey literature, which may have disproportionately excluded locally published research and underestimated the contributions of some dengue-endemic countries. Furthermore, publication counts were not normalized against national population sizes or total national research expenditures, and bibliometric metrics reflect publication frequency rather than study quality or causal validity. Despite these limitations, the evidence underscores that while scientific attention toward dengue and extreme weather is expanding, international partnerships, surveillance infrastructure, and local research investments must be directed toward under-represented endemic settings facing high climatic suitability and rapidly escalating epidemiological burdens. analysis.brief_en: This news report discusses a bibliometric analysis of global scientific literature on dengue fever and its relationship with climate factors. The study, conducted between 2008 and May 2026, found that while research on meteorological drivers of dengue transmission has grown significantly since 2020, it does not align with the current disease burden or long-term trends in incidence rates. The research, which evaluated 290 publications, revealed that scientific productivity is heavily concentrated in a few well-resourced nations, despite the widespread transmission of dengue across 90 countries and territories. The findings highlight a geographic mismatch in research efforts, leaving several regions with high transmission potential and severe public health burdens underrepresented in international scientific publications. The study underscores the complex interplay between climate variables and dengue transmission dynamics, emphasizing the need for more equitable research distribution to address global health challenges effectively.

news.content_zh: 本新闻报道讨论了对 登革热 的全球科学文献及其与气候因素的关系的文献计量分析。这项研究于 2008 年至 2026 年 5 月期间进行,发现虽然自 2020 年以来对登革热 传播 气象驱动因素的研究显着增长,但它与当前的疾病负担或 发病率 发病率的长期趋势不一致。这项研究对 290 种出版物进行了评估,结果显示,尽管登革热在 90 个国家和地区广泛传播,但科学生产力主要集中在少数资源丰富的国家。研究结果凸显了研究工作的地理不匹配,导致一些具有高潜力和严重公共卫生负担的地区在国际科学出版物中的代表性不足。该研究强调了气候变量与登革热传播动态之间复杂的相互作用,强调需要更公平的研究分配以有效应对全球健康挑战。

news.content: Kazinform Kazakhstan Regions Society Law and Order Culture Sport President Politics President Government Parliament International Relations Economy Analytics World Central Asia Eurasia Middle East America Africa EN KZ QZ РУ EN 中文 ЎЗ ق ز kz qz ру en 中文 ўз ق ز Kazakhstan Regions Society Law and Order Culture Sport President Politics President Government Parliament International Relations Economy Analytics World Central Asia Eurasia Middle East America Africa Kazakhstan reports 14 imported cases of dengue fever since start of 2026 21:14, 25 November 2026 Fourteen imported cases of dengue fever have been registered in Kazakhstan since the beginning of 2026. The disease was detected in people returning from abroad, including the Maldives, Vietnam and India, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports. Photo source: Unsplash Speaking at a briefing at the Central Communications Service, Sarkhat Beissenova, Chair of the Committee for Sanitary and Epidemiological Control of Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Health, said seven cases had been recorded in Almaty among people arriving from the Maldives, while two patients had traveled to Vietnam. One case each was linked to trips to India and Dubai. In Astana, the disease was detected in people returning from Vietnam and Indonesia. Another case was registered in Kostanay region in a person who had traveled to Vietnam. Beisenova said that no new cases had been reported in November. In addition, Kazakhstan has recorded five imported cases of malaria since the start of the year. Four were detected in Almaty and one in Astana. Four patients were diagnosed with Plasmodium falciparum malaria, while one had Plasmodium vivax malaria. All cases were laboratory-confirmed. The patients had traveled to African countries, including Uganda, Ghana, Gabon and Zanzibar. In one case, the patient arrived from Vietnam, Beissenova said. She also urged Kazakhstanis to prepare in advance when traveling to countries where infectious diseases are reported and to observe precautionary measures. Earlier, Qazinform reported acute respiratory infections declined 28% in Kazakhstan.
