news.content_title: Take proactive measures to prevent the disease and be vigilant for dengue fever complications.
news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế Take proactive measures to prevent the disease and be vigilant for dengue fever complications. Dengue fever is on the rise, with alarming numbers of cases and deaths. Notably, this disease is no longer just a concern for young children or those with underlying health conditions. Hà Nội Mới•22/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Caring for a dengue fever patient with severe symptoms at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases. Photo: Provided by the hospital. In reality, many adults, including young, healthy individuals without underlying health conditions, still experience shock, severe bleeding, liver and kidney damage, and multi-organ failure. In particular, dangerous complications can arise at the very moment when the illness seems to be subsiding, when the patient's fever begins to subside. Do n't wait for complications to arise before seeking medical attention. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA According to the Department of Disease Prevention ( Ministry of Health ), in the first 10 months of 2026, the whole country recorded more than 170,000 cases of dengue fever, a 1.3-fold increase compared to the same period in 2025, including 21 deaths. Not only has the number of cases increased, but the disease is also becoming more complex. Many adults, even young people who were previously completely healthy, have fallen into critical condition and require intensive treatment due to shock, blood clotting disorders, and multi-organ damage. A typical case is patient PL (23 years old, from Hanoi), who was previously completely healthy but was hospitalized after 7 days of high fever, chills, headache, abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. Despite treatment at another medical facility, her condition worsened. Upon transfer to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, the patient's platelet count had dropped to 21 G/L, liver enzymes were elevated, and she had severe liver damage. Another case involves patient LTS (23 years old, from Tuyen Quang province), who was previously healthy but quickly deteriorated after contracting dengue fever. The patient suffered from hypotension, respiratory failure, liver and kidney damage, and blood clotting disorders. Doctors had to use an extracorporeal oxygenation (ECMO) system combined with hemodialysis to save the patient's life. Based on the severe cases mentioned above, Dr. Pham Van Phuc, Deputy Director of the Intensive Care Unit (National Hospital for Tropical Diseases), noted that one of the reasons patients easily misjudge the severity of dengue fever is overemphasizing the low platelet count. This is a common symptom, but the severity of the disease cannot be determined solely based on the platelet count. Assessing the risk of complications must be based on the overall clinical condition and many other indicators, such as signs of bleeding, blood pressure, pulse, urine output, blood concentration, and organ damage. You may also like According to Dr. Pham Van Phuc, dengue fever has a particularly dangerous characteristic that many people often overlook: the disease can worsen precisely when the fever begins to subside. The critical phase usually occurs between the 3rd and 7th day after onset. At this time, the patient may experience plasma leakage, severe bleeding, or organ damage. If severe plasma leakage is not detected and treated promptly, circulatory volume can decrease, leading to shock, multi-organ failure, and death. Dr. Huynh Tran An Khuong, a medical specialist at the VNVC Vaccination System, also warned that many people are still complacent, believing that dengue fever is only dangerous for young children, so they self-medicate at home or delay seeking medical attention. In particular, when the fever subsides, patients easily mistakenly believe they have recovered, while this could be the time when the fever is subsiding. The disease is starting to become dangerous. Eliminate mosquitoes, prevent the risk of serious illness. According to health experts, dengue fever is now tending to circulate year-round in many localities, instead of being concentrated in a specific epidemic season as before. Notably, all four dengue virus types that cause the disease, including DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4, are recorded as circulating. The simultaneous presence of multiple virus types means that the risk of infection, reinfection, and complicated disease progression is always present. Dr. Huynh Tran An Khuong noted that people who have previously had dengue fever can still be reinfected because long-term immunity is mainly formed against the specific virus type they were infected with, while cross-protection against other types is usually temporary. In particular, when reinfected with a different virus type, patients may face a higher risk of more severe illness due to antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE). However, not all cases of reinfection lead to a serious illness. Besides being vigilant about the risk of reinfection, people also need to recognize the correct progression of the disease to avoid missing the right time for intervention. Dr. Pham Van Phuc noted that people with or suspected of having dengue fever should immediately go to a medical facility if they experience warning signs such as severe or continuous abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, lethargy, restlessness, nosebleeds, bleeding gums, decreased urination, cold hands and feet, or extreme fatigue. These are symptoms that should not be self-monitored at home, as they may indicate a worsening condition and require prompt assessment and treatment by a doctor. For cases where home monitoring and treatment are prescribed by a doctor, patients need to rest, drink plenty of fluids, and closely monitor their temperature, appetite, urine output, and any unusual symptoms. Medication use must also strictly follow professional instructions; under no circumstances should you increase the dosage of fever-reducing medication or use anti-inflammatory drugs without a prescription, as some medications can increase the risk of bleeding in dengue fever patients. You may also like In addition, patients need to attend follow-up appointments as scheduled, undergo tests as prescribed, and maintain monitoring throughout the period of risk of worsening condition. Even when the fever subsides and symptoms improve, patients should not stop monitoring or assume they have fully recovered. Given the complex situation surrounding dengue fever, health experts advise people to proactively take preventive measures to limit the risk of community spread. Important measures include: eliminating stagnant water sources, destroying mosquito larvae, maintaining a clean living environment, and avoiding mosquito bites. In addition, dengue fever vaccination is a preventive measure that can be considered as directed by healthcare professionals and according to the regulations of the vaccination facility. The combination of mosquito control, appropriate vaccination, and early detection of warning signs will contribute to reducing the risk of contracting the disease and limiting dangerous complications. Do n't wait for complications to arise before seeking medical attention. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA According to the Department of Disease Prevention ( Ministry of Health ), in the first 10 months of 2026, the whole country recorded more than 170,000 cases of dengue fever, a 1.3-fold increase compared to the same period in 2025, including 21 deaths. Not only has the number of cases increased, but the disease is also becoming more complex. Many adults, even young people who were previously completely healthy, have fallen into critical condition and require intensive treatment due to shock, blood clotting disorders, and multi-organ damage. A typical case is patient PL (23 years old, from Hanoi), who was previously completely healthy but was hospitalized after 7 days of high fever, chills, headache, abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. Despite treatment at another medical facility, her condition worsened. Upon transfer to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, the patient's platelet count had dropped to 21 G/L, liver enzymes were elevated, and she had severe liver damage. Another case involves patient LTS (23 years old, from Tuyen Quang province), who was previously healthy but quickly deteriorated after contracting dengue fever. The patient suffered from hypotension, respiratory failure, liver and kidney damage, and blood clotting disorders. Doctors had to use an extracorporeal oxygenation (ECMO) system combined with hemodialysis to save the patient's life. Based on the severe cases mentioned above, Dr. Pham Van Phuc, Deputy Director of the Intensive Care Unit (National Hospital for Tropical Diseases), noted that one of the reasons patients easily misjudge the severity of dengue fever is overemphasizing the low platelet count. This is a common symptom, but the severity of the disease cannot be determined solely based on the platelet count. Assessing the risk of complications must be based on the overall clinical condition and many other indicators, such as signs of bleeding, blood pressure, pulse, urine output, blood concentration, and organ damage. You may also like According to Dr. Pham Van Phuc, dengue fever has a particularly dangerous characteristic that many people often overlook: the disease can worsen precisely when the fever begins to subside. The critical phase usually occurs between the 3rd and 7th day after onset. At this time, the patient may experience plasma leakage, severe bleeding, or organ damage. If severe plasma leakage is not detected and treated promptly, circulatory volume can decrease, leading to shock, multi-organ failure, and death. Dr. Huynh Tran An Khuong, a medical specialist at the VNVC Vaccination System, also warned that many people are still complacent, believing that dengue fever is only dangerous for young children, so they self-medicate at home or delay seeking medical attention. In particular, when the fever subsides, patients easily mistakenly believe they have recovered, while this could be the time when the fever is subsiding. The disease is starting to become dangerous. Eliminate mosquitoes, prevent the risk of serious illness. According to health experts, dengue fever is now tending to circulate year-round in many localities, instead of being concentrated in a specific epidemic season as before. Notably, all four dengue virus types that cause the disease, including DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4, are recorded as circulating. The simultaneous presence of multiple virus types means that the risk of infection, reinfection, and complicated disease progression is always present. Dr. Huynh Tran An Khuong noted that people who have previously had dengue fever can still be reinfected because long-term immunity is mainly formed against the specific virus type they were infected with, while cross-protection against other types is usually temporary. In particular, when reinfected with a different virus type, patients may face a higher risk of more severe illness due to antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE). However, not all cases of reinfection lead to a serious illness. Besides being vigilant about the risk of reinfection, people also need to recognize the correct progression of the disease to avoid missing the right time for intervention. Dr. Pham Van Phuc noted that people with or suspected of having dengue fever should immediately go to a medical facility if they experience warning signs such as severe or continuous abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, lethargy, restlessness, nosebleeds, bleeding gums, decreased urination, cold hands and feet, or extreme fatigue. These are symptoms that should not be self-monitored at home, as they may indicate a worsening condition and require prompt assessment and treatment by a doctor. For cases where home monitoring and treatment are prescribed by a doctor, patients need to rest, drink plenty of fluids, and closely monitor their temperature, appetite, urine output, and any unusual symptoms. Medication use must also strictly follow professional instructions; under no circumstances should you increase the dosage of fever-reducing medication or use anti-inflammatory drugs without a prescription, as some medications can increase the risk of bleeding in dengue fever patients. You may also like In addition, patients need to attend follow-up appointments as scheduled, undergo tests as prescribed, and maintain monitoring throughout the period of risk of worsening condition. Even when the fever subsides and symptoms improve, patients should not stop monitoring or assume they have fully recovered. Given the complex situation surrounding dengue fever, health experts advise people to proactively take preventive measures to limit the risk of community spread. Important measures include: eliminating stagnant water sources, destroying mosquito larvae, maintaining a clean living environment, and avoiding mosquito bites. In addition, dengue fever vaccination is a preventive measure that can be considered as directed by healthcare professionals and according to the regulations of the vaccination facility. The combination of mosquito control, appropriate vaccination, and early detection of warning signs will contribute to reducing the risk of contracting the disease and limiting dangerous complications. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Immunocompromised Adults Face Higher Risk of Severe Dengue by November 25, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Immunocompromised Adults Face Higher Risk of Severe Dengue Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In a multicenter retrospective cohort study examining laboratory-confirmed dengue infections, researchers found that immunocompromised adults faced a substantially higher risk of developing severe dengue compared to non-immunocompromised patients. The investigation evaluated hospital records between January 2023 and June 2024 to address the lack of large comparative cohorts evaluating dengue severity in individuals with compromised immune defenses. The study included 894 patients diagnosed with dengue, of whom 59 met specific clinical criteria for immunocompromised status. Qualifying conditions included living with HIV with CD4 counts below 350 cells per microliter, having received a solid organ transplant or a hematopoietic stem cell transplant within the preceding two years, active malignancy, asplenia or splenectomy, and medical regimens requiring immunosuppressive medications. Demographic analysis revealed that immunocompromised patients were significantly older, presenting with a median age of 47.0 years compared to 33.5 years in the non-immunocompromised group. Additionally, these patients carried a higher baseline burden of preexisting health conditions, reflected in a median Charlson comorbidity index of 1 versus 0 among non-immunocompromised individuals. While primary clinical features at initial presentation were largely similar, an absence of fever was noted more frequently in the immunocompromised cohort, occurring in 10.2 percent compared to 1.1 percent. Routine laboratory values appeared comparable upon admission, yet immunocompromised patients subsequently exhibited significantly lower nadir platelet counts and prolonged thrombocytopenia throughout their illness. Primary clinical endpoints showed marked disparities, with severe dengue according to World Health Organization 2009 criteria documented in 22 percent of immunocompromised individuals compared to only 4.9 percent of non-immunocompromised patients. Patients with impaired immunity also experienced higher rates of hospital admission, longer stays, and increased 30-day mortality. In multivariable analysis, immunocompromised status and comorbidity index were both independently associated with severe dengue, yielding an odds ratio of 3.43 for immune impairment and 1.33 for the comorbidity score. The researchers concluded that these findings provide critical evidence demonstrating an elevated risk of severe outcomes, highlighting the urgent need for improved strategies for prevention and clinical management in this population. The investigation evaluated hospital records between January 2023 and June 2024 to address the lack of large comparative cohorts evaluating dengue severity in individuals with compromised immune defenses. The study included 894 patients diagnosed with dengue, of whom 59 met specific clinical criteria for immunocompromised status. Qualifying conditions included living with HIV with CD4 counts below 350 cells per microliter, having received a solid organ transplant or a hematopoietic stem cell transplant within the preceding two years, active malignancy, asplenia or splenectomy, and medical regimens requiring immunosuppressive medications. Demographic analysis revealed that immunocompromised patients were significantly older, presenting with a median age of 47.0 years compared to 33.5 years in the non-immunocompromised group. Additionally, these patients carried a higher baseline burden of preexisting health conditions, reflected in a median Charlson comorbidity index of 1 versus 0 among non-immunocompromised individuals. While primary clinical features at initial presentation were largely similar, an absence of fever was noted more frequently in the immunocompromised cohort, occurring in 10.2 percent compared to 1.1 percent. Routine laboratory values appeared comparable upon admission, yet immunocompromised patients subsequently exhibited significantly lower nadir platelet counts and prolonged thrombocytopenia throughout their illness. Primary clinical endpoints showed marked disparities, with severe dengue according to World Health Organization 2009 criteria documented in 22 percent of immunocompromised individuals compared to only 4.9 percent of non-immunocompromised patients. Patients with impaired immunity also experienced higher rates of hospital admission, longer stays, and increased 30-day mortality. In multivariable analysis, immunocompromised status and comorbidity index were both independently associated with severe dengue, yielding an odds ratio of 3.43 for immune impairment and 1.33 for the comorbidity score. The researchers concluded that these findings provide critical evidence demonstrating an elevated risk of severe outcomes, highlighting the urgent need for improved strategies for prevention and clinical management in this population. news.content: Edition IN IN US UK GCC English English हिन्दी मराठी ಕನ್ನಡ தமிழ் বাংলা മലയാളം తెలుగు ગુજરાતી Weather Sign In TOI Science Nature Archaeology Wildlife Earth Space Discovery Today's ePaper Live News Science News Brazil study finds 69% fewer dengue, chikungunya infections with modified mosquitoes Brazil study finds 69% fewer dengue, chikungunya infections with modified mosquitoes Edited by Vijaya Srivastava / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Nov 21, 2026, 21:38 IST Save Comments Share Aa +Text Size Small Medium Large Print File photo of a mosquito feeling on hand (AP Photo/Rick Bowmer, File) Scientists have reported strong new evidence that specially bred mosquitoes carrying a naturally occurring bacteria can significantly reduce the spread of dengue and chikungunya, after a major study involving more than 5,700 children in Brazil found a nearly 69 per cent drop in infections in areas where the mosquitoes were released.The four-year study, conducted in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, found that children living in neighbourhoods with these mosquitoes were far less likely to contract the two mosquito-borne viruses than those in similar areas without them. The protection remained effective even during Brazil's severe dengue outbreak in 2024, researchers said on Saturday.The findings were presented at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. They offer fresh support for using Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes as an alternative to relying only on pesticides and measures to prevent mosquito bites.“This is really exciting,” said Dr David Hamer, a global health expert at Boston University who was not involved in the study.He said combining the release of Wolbachia mosquitoes with existing mosquito-control measures could “knock dengue down to much lower levels” in many places. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like Undo The findings come as Florida faces an unusually large dengue outbreak, which appears to be the biggest recorded in any US state since at least the 1940s.Dengue cases in the continental US are usually linked to international travel. However, Florida health officials had recorded more than 650 locally acquired infections as of Friday. About three-quarters of these cases were reported in Hillsborough County, which includes Tampa. How the mosquito strategy works The approach involves breeding mosquitoes with Wolbachia, a type of bacteria that occurs naturally in many insects. The bacteria are harmless to humans but are not commonly found in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which spread dengue.Wolbachia significantly reduces the mosquitoes' ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes also pass the bacteria on to their offspring.Scientists release both male and female mosquitoes carrying the bacteria into a targeted area. As they breed with the local mosquito population, Wolbachia gradually becomes established. This reduces the ability of the wider mosquito population to spread viruses.The nonprofit World Mosquito Program has been leading efforts to develop and expand this approach outside the US. Earlier field trials in Indonesia and other locations have also shown significant reductions in dengue cases. What the Brazil study found The latest research went beyond tracking reported infections. Researchers tested children's blood for evidence of dengue, chikungunya and Zika infections. This helped identify infections that may have gone undiagnosed because people experienced only mild symptoms.The study followed more than 5,700 children over four years. All participating neighbourhoods received the same pesticide treatments and other mosquito-control measures. Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines However, researchers randomly selected half of the neighbourhoods to receive releases of Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes. They then compared infection rates between children living in the two groups of neighbourhoods.The results showed about a 69 per cent reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections among children in areas where the specially bred mosquitoes were released.Researchers could not establish whether the strategy reduced Zika infections because there were too few cases to draw a reliable conclusion. news.content_original: Edition IN IN US UK GCC English English हिन्दी मराठी ಕನ್ನಡ தமிழ் বাংলা മലയാളം తెలుగు ગુજરાતી Weather Sign In TOI Science Nature Archaeology Wildlife Earth Space Discovery Today's ePaper Live News Science News Brazil study finds 69% fewer dengue, chikungunya infections with modified mosquitoes Brazil study finds 69% fewer dengue, chikungunya infections with modified mosquitoes Edited by Vijaya Srivastava / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Nov 21, 2026, 21:38 IST Save Comments Share Aa +Text Size Small Medium Large Print File photo of a mosquito feeling on hand (AP Photo/Rick Bowmer, File) Scientists have reported strong new evidence that specially bred mosquitoes carrying a naturally occurring bacteria can significantly reduce the spread of dengue and chikungunya, after a major study involving more than 5,700 children in Brazil found a nearly 69 per cent drop in infections in areas where the mosquitoes were released.The four-year study, conducted in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, found that children living in neighbourhoods with these mosquitoes were far less likely to contract the two mosquito-borne viruses than those in similar areas without them. The protection remained effective even during Brazil's severe dengue outbreak in 2024, researchers said on Saturday.The findings were presented at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. They offer fresh support for using Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes as an alternative to relying only on pesticides and measures to prevent mosquito bites.“This is really exciting,” said Dr David Hamer, a global health expert at Boston University who was not involved in the study.He said combining the release of Wolbachia mosquitoes with existing mosquito-control measures could “knock dengue down to much lower levels” in many places. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like Undo The findings come as Florida faces an unusually large dengue outbreak, which appears to be the biggest recorded in any US state since at least the 1940s.Dengue cases in the continental US are usually linked to international travel. However, Florida health officials had recorded more than 650 locally acquired infections as of Friday. About three-quarters of these cases were reported in Hillsborough County, which includes Tampa. How the mosquito strategy works The approach involves breeding mosquitoes with Wolbachia, a type of bacteria that occurs naturally in many insects. The bacteria are harmless to humans but are not commonly found in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which spread dengue.Wolbachia significantly reduces the mosquitoes' ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes also pass the bacteria on to their offspring.Scientists release both male and female mosquitoes carrying the bacteria into a targeted area. As they breed with the local mosquito population, Wolbachia gradually becomes established. This reduces the ability of the wider mosquito population to spread viruses.The nonprofit World Mosquito Program has been leading efforts to develop and expand this approach outside the US. Earlier field trials in Indonesia and other locations have also shown significant reductions in dengue cases. What the Brazil study found The latest research went beyond tracking reported infections. Researchers tested children's blood for evidence of dengue, chikungunya and Zika infections. This helped identify infections that may have gone undiagnosed because people experienced only mild symptoms.The study followed more than 5,700 children over four years. All participating neighbourhoods received the same pesticide treatments and other mosquito-control measures. They then compared infection rates between children living in the two groups of neighbourhoods.The results showed about a 69 per cent reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections among children in areas where the specially bred mosquitoes were released.Researchers could not establish whether the strategy reduced Zika infections because there were too few cases to draw a reliable conclusion. The investigation evaluated hospital records between January 2023 and June 2024 to address the lack of large comparative cohorts evaluating dengue severity in individuals with compromised immune defenses. The study included 894 patients diagnosed with dengue, of whom 59 met specific clinical criteria for immunocompromised status. Qualifying conditions included living with HIV with CD4 counts below 350 cells per microliter, having received a solid organ transplant or a hematopoietic stem cell transplant within the preceding two years, active malignancy, asplenia or splenectomy, and medical regimens requiring immunosuppressive medications. Demographic analysis revealed that immunocompromised patients were significantly older, presenting with a median age of 47.0 years compared to 33.5 years in the non-immunocompromised group. Additionally, these patients carried a higher baseline burden of preexisting health conditions, reflected in a median Charlson comorbidity index of 1 versus 0 among non-immunocompromised individuals. While primary clinical features at initial presentation were largely similar, an absence of fever was noted more frequently in the immunocompromised cohort, occurring in 10.2 percent compared to 1.1 percent. Routine laboratory values appeared comparable upon admission, yet immunocompromised patients subsequently exhibited significantly lower nadir platelet counts and prolonged thrombocytopenia throughout their illness. Primary clinical endpoints showed marked disparities, with severe dengue according to World Health Organization 2009 criteria documented in 22 percent of immunocompromised individuals compared to only 4.9 percent of non-immunocompromised patients. Patients with impaired immunity also experienced higher rates of hospital admission, longer stays, and increased 30-day mortality. In multivariable analysis, immunocompromised status and comorbidity index were both independently associated with severe dengue, yielding an odds ratio of 3.43 for immune impairment and 1.33 for the comorbidity score. The researchers concluded that these findings provide critical evidence demonstrating an elevated risk of severe outcomes, highlighting the urgent need for improved strategies for prevention and clinical management in this population. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Computational Study Identifies Soy Isoflavone Genistein as Dengue Envelope Inhibitor by November 23, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Computational Study Identifies Soy Isoflavone Genistein as Dengue Envelope Inhibitor Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In a computational investigation published in In Silico Research in Biomedicine, researchers evaluated dozens of natural phytochemicals to identify potential inhibitors capable of targeting the structural envelope protein of the dengue virus across multiple viral lineages. Dengue virus, an enveloped pathogen belonging to the Flaviviridae family, is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Globally, dengue represents an escalating public health crisis across tropical and subtropical territories, including South-east Asia, Latin America, the Pacific Islands, and the Caribbean. Epidemiological assessments recorded by the World Health Organization report that over 390 million people contract dengue annually, resulting in roughly 22,000 fatal outcomes, with the Asian continent bearing approximately 67 percent of all clinical cases. Despite the clinical spectrum ranging from sudden high fever, retro-orbital eye pain, arthralgia, headache, and severe myalgia to life-threatening conditions such as dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome, no targeted antiviral pharmaceuticals are currently approved for clinical therapy. Supportive treatment relies almost entirely on careful fluid balance management to mitigate severe dehydration. To overcome the current therapeutic deficit, investigators have increasingly focused on plant-derived secondary metabolites that display broad-spectrum antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antiviral characteristics. The structural architecture of the dengue virion features an approximately eleven-kilobase single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome that encodes three structural proteins comprising the capsid, membrane, and envelope proteins, along with seven non-structural proteins designated NS1, NS2A, NS2B, NS3, NS4A, NS4B, and NS5. Among these, the surface-exposed envelope glycoprotein plays an indispensable role in mediating infection by facilitating virion attachment to host cell surface receptors and driving subsequent membrane fusion. Structurally, the envelope monomer is organized into three distinct structural units: domain I, which acts as a central hinge orchestrating conformational shifts; domain II, which contains a highly conserved hydrophobic fusion loop responsible for dimerization and host membrane insertion; and domain III, which functions as the primary receptor-binding domain. Because the envelope protein also mediates viral hemagglutination and neutralizes host immunological defenses, disrupting its structural integrity represents a strategic approach for halting infection. The research team devised an integrated in silico screening pipeline that began with the systematic collection of dengue virus envelope protein sequences deposited in the UniProt database across four antigenically distinct serotypes, designated DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. Their sequence retrieval yielded eighteen distinct strains for DENV-1, eleven for DENV-2, five for DENV-3, and eight for DENV-4, representing viral isolates collected over multiple decades from Asia, South America, North America, and Australia. The polypeptide chains displayed an average length of 488 plus or minus 8.09 amino acid residues. To pinpoint structurally conserved target domains across serotypes, the investigators conducted multiple sequence alignment using the ClustalW program within the Clustal Omega suite. Based on previous structural literature, six specific functional pockets and active site ranges were mapped along the envelope sequence: amino acid residues 45 to 65, 110 to 140, 190 to 225, 255 to 290, 300 to 345, and 346 to 390, confirming homologous binding regions shared among diverse geographic variants. Three-dimensional structural models of these peptide segments were subsequently generated using the SWISS-MODEL homology modeling server through BLAST and HHblits template selection algorithms. Model reliability was confirmed through rigorous structural validation criteria, requiring favorable MolProbity scores, Ramachandran plot favored percentages of 98 percent or greater, sequence identities exceeding 40 percent, and QMEAN Z-scores higher than negative 4.0. To eliminate structural redundancy, root-mean-square distance calculations were performed in PyMOL software to determine structural convergence among predicted peptide conformations. This structural filtering selected six representative viral sequences: strain A0A0D4D8J0 for segment 45 to 65, strain A0A0N7H514 for segment 110 to 140, strain A0A0D4D8J0 for segments 190 to 225 and 300 to 345, strain A0A0D4D9E3 for segment 255 to 290, and strain J9WMM0 for segment 346 to 390. Active binding crevices within these peptide models were mapped computationally using the CASTp 3.0 server configured with a default radius probe of 1.4 angstroms. Parallel to the viral target preparation, the researchers compiled a curated library of seventy-one plant-derived bioactive antiviral compounds from peer-reviewed literature, retrieving their canonical SMILES notations and three-dimensional spatial structures from the PubChem chemical database. The entire library underwent rigorous virtual ADMET screening via the ADMETlab 2.0 platform to evaluate human intestinal absorption, cellular permeability, metabolic clearance, half-life parameters, blood-brain barrier penetration, and potential organ toxicities. Drug-likeness was evaluated against Lipinski’s rule of five, which specifies a molecular weight below 500 grams per mole, fewer than three hydrogen-bond donors, fewer than twelve hydrogen-bond acceptors, a octanol-water partition coefficient log P below five, and fewer than twelve rotatable bonds. Four candidate molecules successfully satisfied Lipinski rules, the GlaxoSmithKline criteria, and the Golden Triangle rule: the flavone baicalein, the flavonol quercetin, the sesquiterpene lactone artecanin, and the isoflavone genistein. All four demonstrated favorable Caco-2 cell permeability values exceeding negative 5.15, acceptable human hepatotoxicity and skin sensitization profiles, low mutagenic AMES probabilities, and satisfactory drug clearance rates. Rigid molecular docking simulations were executed using the AutoDock 1.5.6 software package across each of the six designated envelope functional pockets, calculating binding free energy values based on classical thermodynamic principles. A uniform grid box measuring 60 by 60 by 60 grid points was constructed in AutoGrid to calculate electrostatic, van der Waals, and solvation energy grids. Across all evaluated active pockets, the four shortlisted phytochemicals displayed pronounced docking affinities, yet genistein consistently registered the strongest overall binding scores. For pocket 45 to 65, baicalein and quercetin both docked with negative 4.6 kilocalories per mole, artecanin with negative 4.4 kilocalories per mole, and genistein with negative 4.9 kilocalories per mole. In the 110 to 140 pocket, baicalein recorded negative 4.7 kilocalories per mole, while quercetin, artecanin, and genistein achieved negative 5.0 kilocalories per mole. In the 190 to 225 pocket, binding values were negative 6.6 kilocalories per mole for baicalein, negative 7.0 for quercetin, negative 6.4 for artecanin, and negative 7.1 for genistein. Docking continued across the remaining three envelope regions, showing consistent intermolecular affinity. In pocket 255 to 290, baicalein scored negative 5.7 kilocalories per mole, artecanin negative 5.6 kilocalories per mole, and both quercetin and genistein negative 5.9 kilocalories per mole. In pocket 300 to 345, baicalein and genistein reached negative 6.0 kilocalories per mole, while quercetin and artecanin reached negative 5.9 kilocalories per mole. Most notably, within the 346 to 390 pocket, genistein established the strongest overall interaction, reaching a binding energy of negative 7.6 kilocalories per mole, outperforming baicalein at negative 7.1 kilocalories per mole, quercetin at negative 7.0 kilocalories per mole, and artecanin at negative 6.8 kilocalories per mole. Across all tested envelope sites, genistein displayed an average binding affinity of negative 6.06 plus or minus 1.1 kilocalories per mole. Within the high-affinity 346 to 390 site of strain J9WMM0, molecular visualization using Discovery Studio revealed an intricate interactome comprising seven van der Waals contacts with threonine 1, leucine 6, proline 26, glutamic acid 30, serine 31, tyrosine 32, and isoleucine 33, alongside a vital hydrogen bond with glutamine 2, and three pi-alkyl linkages involving arginine 5, alanine 24, and proline 27. To investigate whether this top-performing complex could preserve structural stability in a realistic aqueous environment, the researchers conducted 100-nanosecond molecular dynamics simulations using the GROMACS package under the CHARMM27 force field. The genistein-peptide complex was solvated in an explicit TIP3P water cubic box measuring 90.0 by 90.0 by 90.0 nanometers, neutralized with sodium and chloride counter-ions, and energy-minimized to eliminate steric clashes. Simulations ran at a regulated temperature of 300 Kelvin and atmospheric pressure of 1 atmosphere, utilizing the Nose-Hoover thermostat, the Martyna-Tobias-Klein barostat, and particle mesh Ewald electrostatics with a grid spacing of 0.8 angstroms. Trajectory coordinates were logged every 1000 picoseconds, allowing detailed measurement of root-mean-square deviation, root-mean-square fluctuation, radius of gyration, solvent-accessible surface area, and intermolecular hydrogen bonding throughout the 100-nanosecond duration. Analysis of the simulation trajectories corroborated the structural integrity and conformational stability of the genistein-envelope complex. Root-mean-square deviation of the complex equilibrated during the initial 10 nanoseconds and remained stable between 0.7 and 0.8 nanometers from 20 to 60 nanoseconds. Although a minor elevation toward 1.6 nanometers appeared after 80 nanoseconds, the trajectory re-stabilized near 1.1 nanometers toward the simulation endpoint, confirming persistent ligand containment without displacement from the active pocket. Residue-level root-mean-square fluctuation plots revealed that while terminal peptide ends exhibited expected flexibility near 0.8 nanometers, core interacting residues displayed restrained fluctuations between 0.2 and 0.4 nanometers. Furthermore, the radius of gyration maintained a narrow range of 1.03 to 1.27 nanometers, demonstrating sustained structural compactness. Solvent-accessible surface area values fluctuated steadily between 38 and 48 square nanometers, indicating reliable solvent exposure and stable peptide folding. Intermolecular hydrogen bonding remained resilient, typically exhibiting one to three continuous hydrogen bonds and intermittently reaching four to five contacts, while principal component analysis confirmed tightly clustered conformational dynamics. Thermodynamic stability was further quantified through Molecular Mechanics/Generalized Born Surface Area calculations using the GMX_MMPBSA tool, which revealed a favorable net binding free energy of approximately negative 18 kilocalories per mole. Gas-phase molecular mechanics contributions totaled roughly negative 35 kilocalories per mole, dominated by favorable van der Waals interactions of approximately negative 25 kilocalories per mole and electrostatic interactions contributing negative 10 kilocalories per mole, illustrating strong hydrophobic packing. Although the total polar solvation energy presented an unfavorable barrier of approximately positive 20 kilocalories per mole, it was partly compensated by favorable non-polar solvation of negative 3 kilocalories per mole, ensuring an overall spontaneous binding state. While genistein occurs widely in dietary legumes, particularly mature soybeans yielding between 5.6 and 276 milligrams per 100 grams, the study authors emphasize that their computational findings are strictly dry-lab predictions. Wet-lab experimental investigations, including in vitro viral plaque reduction neutralization assays and subsequent in vivo trials, remain essential before any clinical antiviral therapeutic claims can be established. S. (2026). Active compounds against dengue virus: Genistein as a potent DENV envelope inhibitor through toxicity profiling and interactomics. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Blocking XPO1 Nuclear Export Promotes Dengue Virus Replication in Cultured Cells by November 24, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Blocking XPO1 Nuclear Export Promotes Dengue Virus Replication in Cultured Cells Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Inhibiting exportin 1, a fundamental cellular transport receptor responsible for carrying proteins and ribonucleoprotein complexes out of the nucleus, unexpectedly enhances the replication of dengue virus serotype 2 in human hepatoma cell cultures. In an investigation conducted using Huh-7 human hepatocellular carcinoma cells, researchers evaluated how blocking the exportin 1, or XPO1, nuclear export pathway affects the trafficking of the viral non-structural protein 3, known as NS3, alongside its downstream consequences on mitochondrial dynamics and innate antiviral defenses. Although orthoflavivirus replication cycles operate predominantly within the host cytoplasm in association with membranes derived from the endoplasmic reticulum, viral factors routinely transit into the cellular nucleus. Rather than restricting viral propagation, targeted pharmacological disruption of XPO1-mediated export drove the accumulation of NS3 in both nuclear and mitochondrial compartments, reorganized mitochondrial architecture into elongated networks, and blunted type I interferon secretion, establishing a distinctly pro-viral environment in vitro. The study specifically addressed how nucleocytoplasmic transport mechanics influence the intracellular sorting of dengue virus non-structural protein 3, a multifunctional enzyme possessing essential viral protease and helicase activities required for polyprotein processing and RNA replication. Previous investigations had established that dengue virus proteins, notably the polymerase NS5 and the protease-helicase NS3, utilize classical importin pathways to access the nucleus during the initial phases of infection, where they degrade structural nucleoporins within the nuclear pore complex and interfere with host transcriptional networks. While earlier strategies aimed at blocking nuclear import with compounds such as ivermectin succeeded in restricting viral replication, the precise role played by nuclear export pathways and their structural link to extra-nuclear organelles had remained largely uncharacterized. The research team explored whether obstructing nuclear export would cause dengue virus NS3 to redistribute abnormally between the cell nucleus and the mitochondrial network, and whether this trafficking bottleneck altered organellar integrity and cellular immune competence. To evaluate these transport mechanisms, the scientists propagated dengue virus type 2, using the New Guinea C reference strain, alongside a comparative Zika virus strain, using neonatal CD-1 suckling mouse brains under approved institutional animal care protocols. These neonatal murine brain tissues served strictly as an in vivo viral propagation substrate rather than an animal disease model, yielding clarified viral stocks for downstream cell culture experiments. Cultured human Huh-7 cells, maintained in high-glucose Advanced Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium supplemented with fetal bovine serum and antibiotics, were infected with dengue virus type 2 or Zika virus at a multiplicity of infection of five. Alongside authentic infections, the authors also introduced plasmid constructs encoding dengue virus NS2B-NS3 into uninfected Huh-7 cells through electroporation, permitting the examination of NS3 sorting and mitochondrial alterations independent of the full viral replication cycle or secondary structural proteins. Using transmission immunoelectron microscopy with colloidal gold-labeled antibodies, the investigators systematically mapped the subcellular locations of NS3 in Huh-7 cells at twelve and twenty-four hours post-infection. In cells infected with dengue virus type 2, colloidal gold particles indicating NS3 were clearly resolved not only throughout the cytoplasm and the nucleus but also directly within the interior of mitochondria. Quantitative assessment revealed that 17.5 percent of mitochondria were positive for NS3 gold labeling at twelve hours post-infection, an abundance that expanded to 27.5 percent of mitochondria by twenty-four hours. In sharp contrast, parallel experiments performed in Zika virus-infected Huh-7 cells showed that zero percent of mitochondria contained NS3 gold particles at either time point, even though Zika virus NS3 readily accumulated within the cytoplasm and nucleus. Multiple sequence alignment of orthoflavivirus proteins demonstrated that a defined mitochondrial targeting sequence, previously reported in dengue virus serotype 1 NS3, is preserved across dengue serotypes but lacks sufficient sequence conservation in Zika virus NS3, explaining the striking disparity in organellar tropism between the two viruses. To probe the dependence of NS3 distribution on cellular export mechanisms, the researchers employed two distinct small-molecule inhibitors of XPO1: leptomycin B, an irreversible covalent inhibitor binding cysteine 528 of the transport receptor, and selinexor, a reversible first-generation selective inhibitor of nuclear export developed for clinical oncology. Treatment of Huh-7 cells with 37 nanomolar leptomycin B for twenty-four hours was first validated using indirect immunofluorescence confocal microscopy and subcellular fractionation assays targeting cyclin B1, an endogenous cellular cargo that relies strictly on XPO1 for nuclear clearance. Whereas cyclin B1 remained predominantly cytoplasmic in vehicle-treated controls, leptomycin B caused marked nuclear retention. Western blot analysis of isolated nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions demonstrated that XPO1 inhibition produced a substantial increase of dengue virus NS3 inside the nucleus. Intriguingly, western blots of purified mitochondrial fractions, validated for purity using the mitochondrial marker TOMM22 alongside nuclear and cytoplasmic controls, demonstrated that leptomycin B treatment concurrently elevated NS3 levels within mitochondria, a finding corroborated in electroporated cells expressing recombinant NS2B3. The scientists next determined how pharmacological export blockade altered mitochondrial ultrastructure. Transmission electron microscopy revealed that uninfected, vehicle-treated Huh-7 cells possessed predominantly small, rounded, or short mitochondria. Following twenty-four hours of exposure to either 37 nanomolar leptomycin B or 200 nanomolar selinexor, uninfected cells exhibited pronounced mitochondrial elongation, reflected by statistically significant increases in total mitochondrial cross-sectional area. Two-dimensional morphometric analysis of confocal images stained for TOMM22 confirmed this remodeling, showing substantial rises in mitochondrial surface area, perimeter length, and network branching index following XPO1 inhibition. When Huh-7 cells were infected with dengue virus type 2 in the absence of inhibitors, mitochondria likewise underwent marked elongation compared to uninfected controls, matching previous observations of virus-induced organelle reshaping. While treating infected cells with leptomycin B or selinexor induced thinner mitochondrial profiles and some structural cristae disorganization, the inhibitors did not amplify the overall elongation beyond the pronounced morphological transformation already driven by dengue infection itself. Because mitochondrial remodeling frequently coincides with changes in organelle turnover and mitochondrial biogenesis, the authors examined mitochondrial mass and biogenesis signaling pathways following XPO1 inhibition. Flow cytometry measurements of Huh-7 cells stained for the outer mitochondrial membrane marker TOMM22 showed that while roughly 60 to 70 percent of cells remained positive across all groups, mean fluorescence intensity rose significantly in uninfected cells treated with leptomycin B or selinexor, indicating an increase in overall mitochondrial mass at the population level. Flow cytometry also revealed that the frequency of dengue-infected cells, identified by intracellular NS3 positivity at twenty-four hours post-infection, expanded from 15 percent in vehicle-treated controls to 26 percent following leptomycin B exposure. Total cellular levels of NS3 protein rose in parallel on western blots. When investigating peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha, or PGC1-alpha, the master transcriptional regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis, researchers detected a modest, non-significant trend toward elevated protein abundance in treated cells and a transient increase in PGC1-alpha messenger RNA in mock-infected cultures, suggesting that biogenesis pathways may be modestly engaged but remain preliminary under these experimental settings. The downstream consequences of nuclear export blockade directly favored viral proliferation rather than antiviral defense. Transmission electron microscopy of dengue virus-infected Huh-7 cells treated with leptomycin B or selinexor revealed a pronounced proliferation of virus-induced cytoplasmic replication vesicles compared to untreated infected cells. Plaque-forming unit assays conducted on cell culture supernatants showed that both leptomycin B and selinexor significantly increased the output of infectious dengue virus type 2 virions. Quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction assays measuring intracellular viral genomes demonstrated an approximate two-fold increase in viral RNA copies following leptomycin B exposure and a six-fold increase in cells treated with selinexor. Notably, this pro-viral enhancement was entirely specific to dengue virus; parallel viral yield assays and focus-forming unit titrations carried out in Zika virus-infected Huh-7 cells showed no significant alterations in infectious particle release or viral RNA accumulation after XPO1 inhibition. To resolve how blocking nuclear export accelerated dengue replication despite triggering cellular stress, the investigators examined the modulation of the type I interferon signaling cascade. Unstimulated Huh-7 cells exhibited minimal baseline interferon activation, prompting the team to pre-stimulate cells with twenty micrograms per milliliter of recombinant human interferon-beta for six hours before virus inoculation. Pre-stimulated cells were subsequently infected with dengue virus type 2 and treated with vehicle, leptomycin B, or selinexor for twenty-four hours. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays performed on cell culture supernatants revealed that pre-stimulated, infected cells treated with either nuclear export inhibitor suffered an approximate 50 percent decrease in secreted interferon-beta protein compared to untreated stimulated controls. Paradoxically, quantitative reverse-transcription PCR demonstrated a two- to four-fold elevation in interferon-beta and interferon-stimulated gene IFI44L transcripts across treated cells, indicating that while transcription was initiated, post-transcriptional stages such as mRNA nuclear export, protein translation, or cytokine secretion were severely disrupted by XPO1 inhibition. This sharp reduction in functional interferon-beta secretion directly uncoupled the host cell’s antiviral defense from viral control. In untreated Huh-7 cells, interferon-beta pre-stimulation successfully suppressed dengue virus type 2 particle release into the culture medium. However, when cells were treated with leptomycin B or selinexor, infectious viral titers increased significantly even in the presence of prior interferon priming, overcoming the established antiviral state. The authors contextualize these results by noting that while selinexor promotes proteasomal degradation of XPO1 and leptomycin B covalently modifies the receptor without reducing total XPO1 abundance, both agents elicited matching increases in viral titer, NS3 organellar redistribution, and suppression of cytokine output. The researchers caution that these findings are derived from in vitro human hepatoma cell cultures and neonatal mouse brain propagation stocks, meaning clinical extrapolations regarding selective nuclear export inhibitors in human dengue pathology must account for complex tissue-specific immune responses and differences in viral replication kinetics across distinct host systems. supplementary_news.content: Florida Dengue Cases Reach 651, Experts Warn About Mosquitoes Breeding in Backyards Florida homeowners may have more to worry about than weeds and pests hiding in their gardens. A growing dengue outbreak has brought new attention to the small pools of standing water where disease-carrying mosquitoes can breed, including places people might overlook during routine yard maintenance. According to the latest Florida Department of Health surveillance figures, the state has recorded 651 locally acquired dengue cases across 12 counties in 2026. The outbreak is the largest reported in the continental United States in decades, with infections far exceeding Florida's previous annual record of 199 cases in 2023. The outbreak has been concentrated around Tampa Bay, with Hillsborough County accounting for 487 cases and neighboring Pinellas County reporting 116 as of November 14. Although the latest weekly figures suggest infections may be slowing, Hillsborough County has extended its local state of emergency through November 26. Health experts also warn that official case counts may underestimate the true number of infections. For residents, the concern extends beyond neighborhoods with confirmed cases. The mosquito species responsible for much of dengue transmission can reproduce around ordinary homes, turning flowerpot saucers, clogged gutters, and forgotten outdoor containers into potential breeding sites. Hidden Around Homes Embedded media follows; please allow a moment to load. Unlike mosquitoes associated with large ponds or marshes, Aedes aegypti, a major mosquito species responsible for dengue transmission, is well adapted to living near people. It lays eggs along the inside walls of containers that collect water, making residential properties suitable places for reproduction. Kevin Sukovich, a licensed pest control operator who owns Clermont-based Webenex, told the Clermont Sun that homeowners play an important role in controlling these mosquitoes, even when county crews are spraying public areas. "The county can spray the streets, but this mosquito breeds in a bottle cap of water behind your grill," Sukovich said. "Nobody owns that part. The homeowner does." The CDC recommends inspecting outdoor spaces at least once a week. Birdbaths, buckets, children's toys, discarded tires, and flowerpot saucers should be emptied and scrubbed to remove mosquito eggs. Simply pouring out the water may leave eggs attached to the container. Gardeners should pay particular attention to areas where water collects unnoticed. Rain barrels need tight-fitting covers or fine mesh screens, while gutters should be kept clear so water can drain. Water-holding plants and containers also deserve attention, especially in shaded sections of the yard. Beyond Backyard Spraying Removing breeding sites is an important first step, but it does not eliminate every mosquito already living around a property. According to CDC mosquito-control guidance, adult mosquitoes can shelter in dark, humid locations, including beneath patio furniture and around garages. Targeted insecticide treatments may help control them, although products must be used according to their labels. For water that cannot be drained or covered, the agency recommends appropriately labeled mosquito larvicides. These target immature mosquitoes before they become flying adults. Homeowners should select products intended for the particular location rather than applying pesticides indiscriminately around ornamental plants, wildlife habitats, or water features. Personal protection matters, too. Aedes mosquitoes can bite during daylight hours, meaning gardeners are not necessarily safe just because they avoid going outside at dusk. EPA-registered insect repellents, long sleeves, and well-maintained window screens can reduce exposure while residents work outdoors or relax on patios. When Bites Become Serious Dengue can cause fever, severe headaches, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, and rashes. However, not everyone who becomes infected develops noticeable symptoms. Health experts caution that reported cases may underestimate the outbreak's true extent because some infections cause mild symptoms or no symptoms at all. Reporting delays can also make it difficult to measure the outbreak while cases are being investigated. According to WUSF's November 20 report, Florida recorded 27 additional locally acquired cases during the latest reporting week, down from 100 in the preceding report. Although most people with symptomatic dengue recover, the infection can occasionally progress to severe illness involving bleeding, fluid leakage, or shock. The CDC advises seeking emergency medical care for warning signs such as persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, or unusual bleeding, particularly after a fever begins to subside. There is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue. The CDC recommends rest, adequate fluids, and acetaminophen to help manage fever and pain. People who have or may have dengue should avoid aspirin and ibuprofen because these medications can increase the risk of bleeding. Anyone who suspects they have dengue should contact a healthcare professional for evaluation and guidance. Preventing the Problem For Florida homeowners, preventing mosquito bites begins with paying attention to the places where mosquitoes reproduce. A forgotten bucket, clogged gutter, or water-filled flowerpot saucer can provide breeding conditions even in an otherwise well-maintained yard. With hundreds of locally acquired dengue infections already reported this year, a weekly inspection of outdoor spaces is a simple precaution worth taking. Removing standing water, maintaining screens, and using appropriate insect repellent can help reduce exposure while residents continue enjoying their gardens. Want more articles like this one? supplementary_news.content: Schedule NFL News Draft Fantasy Odds Betting Newsletter Shop NEWS Dengue cases climb again in Florida. See county-by county numbers Cheryl McCloud Sarah Perkel C. A. Bridges USA TODAY Updated Nov. 23, 2026, 9:50 a.m. ET More than 600 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported this year in Florida, according to the Florida Department of Health's Weekly Arbovirus Surveillance Report. The report for the period from Nov. 8 through Nov. 14 says that "651 cases of locally acquired dengue and 22 mosquito pools have been reported from 12 counties" in 2026. From Nov. 8 through Nov. 14 alone, 27 cases of locally acquired dengue were reported in Florida. More than 600 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported this year in Florida, according to the Florida Department of Health's Weekly Arbovirus Surveillance Report. The report for the period from Nov. 8 through Nov. 14 says that "651 cases of locally acquired dengue and 22 mosquito pools have been reported from 12 counties" in 2026. From Nov. 8 through Nov. 14 alone, 27 cases of locally acquired dengue were reported in Florida. Hillsborough County saw 487 of the 651 reported locally acquired dengue cases this year. Brevard County saw one case, Broward County saw one case, Citrus County saw three cases, Manatee County saw two cases, Miami-Dade saw 16 cases, Orange County saw 15 cases, Palm Beach County saw one case, Pasco County saw six cases, Pinellas County saw 116 cases, Polk County saw one case and Seminole County saw two cases. Florida's outbreak far exceeds the previous largest outbreak, which was 264 local cases in Hawaii's Big Island between September 2015 and March 2016. Dengue is also known as dengue fever or breakbone fever, the latter due to the pain it can cause. It can present as "a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain," along with fever and "sometimes" a rash, according to the Florida Department of Health in Miami-Dade County. Symptoms of dengue will appear within 14 days of being bitten by an infected mosquito. Dengue is not contagious, and is transmitted via the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. Dengue cases continue to climb in Florida According to Florida Department of Health data released Nov. 14, 12 counties have reported 651 locally acquired dengue cases, up from 624 reported Nov. 13. One new case of west Nile virus was reported over the past week in Holmes County. Dengue: 651 cases 487 in Hillsborough County 116 in Pinellas County 16 in Miami-Dade County 15 in Orange County 6 in Pasco County 3 in Citrus County 2 in Manatee County 2 in Seminole County 1 in Brevard County 1 in Broward County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: 10 cases 2 in Alachua County 2 in Duval County (including one asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Columbia County 2 in Holmes County 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Sarasota County 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 2 cases 2 in Miami-Dade County Eastern Equine Encephalitis: 1 case 1 in Leon County How to best prevent mosquito-borne illnesses In June, Miami-Dade County encouraged residents to "take proactive steps" to prevent the spread of mosquito-borne illnesses, including "frequently checking for and eliminating any standing water." That's the best protection against "container-breeding mosquitoes," said a press release by the county, which are the "likeliest species to transmit the viruses that cause dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever," illnesses that are among those most commonly transmitted by mosquitoes. Standing water usually accumulates after rainfall or irrigation in items like potted planters, saucers, outdoor toys, coolers and boat/car tarps, according to the release. "As little as one teaspoon or bottle cap of water standing for more than one week is enough for mosquitoes to breed and multiply," according to a flyer provided by the FDOH. As for individual protection, mosquito repellent can help prevent bites while outdoors, especially between "dusk and dawn," when mosquitoes are most active. The county also suggests: Covering entrances to one's home, including windows and doors, with mesh screens. Wearing clothes with long sleeves and pant legs to "maximize skin protection." Regularly cleaning rain gutters to avoid water pooling within them. Filling up indentations in one's lawn, air conditioner drain areas and tree holes. Regularly replacing water in outdoor pet dishes and birdbaths. Requesting a mosquito inspection via the county’s online portal. Sarah Perkel is a South Florida Connect Reporter for the USA TODAY Network's Florida Connect team. Telangana reported 10,077 dengue cases and no deaths in 2024, according to the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC).However, the death registry recorded 47 people whose death certificates listed dengue as the cause, highlighting a national mismatch that experts said reflected gaps in disease surveillance and reporting rather than an absence of fatalities.The discrepancy persists over a longer period. Between 2021 and 2025, Telangana reported 46,612 dengue cases, including over 8,000 in 2025.More than 4,000 cases were recorded between April and August this year. Yet, the NCVBDC recorded just one death during the five years from 2021 to 2025.In contrast, the Registrar General’s Medical Certification of Cause of Death (MCCD) reports recorded 270 dengue deaths in Telangana between 2021 and 2024: 45 in 2021, 99 in 2022, 79 in 2023 and 47 in 2024. MCCD data for 2025 is yet to be released.The gap is also evident nationally. The MCCD report recorded 2,340 medically certified dengue deaths in 2024, compared with just 297 in the Union Health Ministry’s NCVBDC surveillance system. The MCCD figure was about 688% higher than the NCVBDC count.Doctors in Hyderabad said dengue cases have increased this year despite relatively weak rainfall. Why the numbers differ? While infections have generally been less severe than last year, fatalities have continued to occur. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like Undo Dr Madap Karuna, a senior paediatrician, said she had come across three dengue deaths — a four-year-old boy with severe comorbidities, a 60-year-old patient and a college student.“We tried to raise funds for the four-year-old boy, who had acute liver failure. We could raise only 50,000, while the treatment required several lakhs. He did not receive the supportive care he needed, and the cost of treatment was enormous. Severe dengue can also lead to complications such as liver failure,” she said. ‘To examine MCCD figures’ Dr Venkat Kumar Nani of Apollo Hospitals said dengue cases had crossed 5,000 this year despite weaker rainfall.“We are seeing many more cases this year, even without heavy rain. Last year, there were fewer cases but more complications. This year, there are more cases, but the severity is lower,” he said.He said he had seen two dengue deaths from Telangana this year and two last year. “I saw four or five dengue patients today alone. In some cases, platelet counts have fallen to around 20,000. Some patients also have to remain hospitalised for extended periods,” he added.Health experts said discrepancies arise partly because many patients with high fever initially approach private clinics, where testing may be limited, and cases are not always reported to the vector-borne disease surveillance system.By the time some patients reach govt hospitals, they may already be in shock or suffering from multiple organ failure.Dr Ravinder Naik, director of Public Health, said suspected but unconfirmed dengue deaths would be investigated, including through verbal autopsies, to establish the cause.“A death is counted in the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) only when it meets the prescribed criteria,” he said. Naik added that the Health Department would also examine the MCCD figures. “We will analyse the data and ask MCCD officials to ensure that no incorrect entries are made at district registrar offices,” he said. OffOn Stream on Scientists report strong new evidence that specially bred mosquitoes can fend off dengue There is new evidence that breeding a special kind of mosquito could help fend off dengue infections, rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten ByLAURAN NEERGAARD AP medical writer November 21, 2026, 12:35 AM WASHINGTON -- Children who lived in Brazilian neighborhoods buzzing with a special kind of mosquito were far less likely to catch dengue or another worrisome virus, chikungunya, researchers reported Saturday. The major study of more than 5,700 children in one of the world’s dengue hot spots offers new evidence that breeding mosquitoes unable to transmit these viruses can be a viable strategy rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten. In neighborhoods populated by these so-called Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes, researchers found about a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections in schoolchildren compared to similar neighborhoods — an effect sustained even during Brazil’s severe 2024 dengue outbreak, said Dr. Sri Edupuganti of Emory University, part of the international research team. The researchers reported the findings at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. “This is really exciting,” said Dr. David Hamer, a global health expert at Boston University who wasn’t involved with the Brazilian study. He predicts that pairing more use of these Wolbachia mosquitoes with existing steps to fight mosquito-borne disease could “knock dengue down to much lower levels” in many places. The latest research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus, what appears to be the biggest in any U.S. state since at least the 1940s. Usually in the continental U.S., dengue is found mostly in people who traveled internationally. But as of Friday, Florida health officials had tallied more than 650 locally acquired cases, about three-quarters of them in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa. Outside the U.S., the nonprofit World Mosquito Program has pioneered the Wolbachia strategy. How it works: Scientists breed mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia. It is harmless to people and common in many insects, although not dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. The bacteria dramatically reduce the mosquitoes’ ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes spread the bacteria to their offspring, so releasing enough of the specially bred insects — males and females — into an area allows Wolbachia to gradually become established in the local mosquito population. But because people with mild symptoms may not be diagnosed, the new study in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, went further. Researchers tested blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya or the Zika virus. The four-year study compared children living in neighborhoods that all got the same pesticide and other mosquito-control interventions, but half were randomly assigned to have Wolbachia mosquitoes released into the area. There were too few cases of Zika to calculate if the special mosquitoes had any effect on that disease. ___ AP Medical Writer Mike Stobbe contributed to this report. ___ The Associated Press’ health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations. Start your Independent Membership today. Join today Already a member? Log in A specially bred mosquito appears to offer strong protection against dengue and chikungunya, according to a new study, as cases of mosquito-borne illnesses spike in Florida. The major study of more than 5,700 children in Brazil, one of the world's dengue hot spots, offers new evidence that breeding mosquitoes unable to transmit viruses can be a viable new strategy instead of relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten. Dr Sri Edupuganti of Emory University, part of the international research team, said children in neighborhoods populated by Wolbachia-carrying insects showed about a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections compared with similar neighborhoods. open image in gallery Scientists bred mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia (Getty Images/iStockphoto) The effect was sustained even during Brazil's severe 2024 dengue outbreak, she said. The findings were reported at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. Florida grapples with large outbreak The latest research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus, what appears to be the biggest in any U.S. state since at least the 1940s. But as of Friday, Florida health officials had tallied more than 650 locally acquired cases, about three-quarters of them in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa. Outside the U.S., the nonprofit World Mosquito Program has pioneered the Wolbachia strategy. Scientists breed mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia. How Wolbachia strategy works The bacteria are harmless to people and common in many insects, although not dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. Wolbachia dramatically reduce the mosquitoes' ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes spread the bacteria to their offspring, so releasing enough of the specially bred insects, males and females, into an area allows Wolbachia to gradually become established in the local mosquito population. Field trials and other studies in Indonesia and elsewhere have shown the strategy can significantly lower dengue diagnoses. But because people with mild symptoms may not be diagnosed, the new study in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, went further. Researchers tested blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya or the Zika virus.
