supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Blood Biomarker Ratio Shows Moderate Accuracy for Detecting Severe Dengue Cases by November 21, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Blood Biomarker Ratio Shows Moderate Accuracy for Detecting Severe Dengue Cases Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating the aspartate aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio index has determined that the blood-based marker demonstrates moderate diagnostic accuracy for identifying severe or complicated dengue. The evaluation focused on synthesizing available evidence to determine how accurately the index reflects severe or complicated conditions based on definitions applied within existing clinical literature. To investigate the performance of the test, investigators conducted a systematic search across seven electronic databases from their inception through March 13, 2026. Eligible studies were required to evaluate the index specifically among patients with laboratory-confirmed dengue infections. The review adhered strictly to the methodological standards outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies guidance. The study selection process identified eight eligible investigations for qualitative synthesis, from which six studies encompassing a total of 948 participants provided sufficient data to be pooled quantitatively. Study-level sensitivity and specificity values were calculated directly from extracted or reconstructed two-by-two contingency tables. Pooled summary estimates were then derived using a frequentist bivariate random-effects Reitsma model fitted via restricted maximum likelihood estimation. Across the pooled primary analysis of six studies, the index yielded a summary sensitivity of 0.75, with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning from 0.66 to 0.82. The corresponding summary specificity was 0.80, with a 95 percent confidence interval ranging from 0.76 to 0.84. In addition, the pooled positive likelihood ratio was estimated at 3.76, while the negative likelihood ratio was 0.32, producing an overall diagnostic odds ratio of 12.42. Evaluation of global discriminative capacity established an area under the summary receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.841. Stability of these statistical results was assessed through leave-one-out sensitivity analyses, which generated comparable performance estimates across iterations. In a separate sensitivity analysis restricted to four studies specifically comparing severe dengue against non-severe dengue, the model calculated a sensitivity of 0.73, a specificity of 0.79, and an area under the curve of 0.821. The researchers cautioned that these pooled accuracy figures reflect a heterogeneous target condition and must not be interpreted as applying exclusively to strictly defined severe dengue classifications. Substantial variation in clinical target definitions alongside a broad range of retrospectively selected index thresholds currently constrain direct clinical applicability. Because retrospective cutoff selection can overestimate diagnostic accuracy, rigorous prospective validation remains essential before the index can be routinely implemented alongside standard clinical assessments and serial laboratory monitoring. In their detailed evaluation of diagnostic performance, the investigators systematically assessed potential heterogeneity and threshold effects across the gathered investigations. supplementary_news.content: Florida reported one new human case of West Nile virus infection in Holmes County during the week of Nov. 8-14, while locally acquired dengue cases and mosquito-borne illness advisories remained widespread across the state. State arbovirus surveillance also recorded 27 locally acquired dengue cases and 29 travel-associated dengue cases this week. No human cases of St. Louis encephalitis or eastern equine encephalitis were reported this week. Sixteen sentinel chickens tested positive for antibodies to West Nile virus in Alachua, Bay, Brevard, Citrus, Hernando, Indian River, Leon, Pasco, Pinellas, Sarasota, Sumter and Walton counties. Two sentinel chickens tested positive for antibodies to eastern equine encephalitis in Bay and Leon counties. Florida had 651 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, with cases reported in Brevard, Broward, Citrus, Hillsborough, Manatee, Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas, Polk and Seminole counties. Hillsborough County had 487 of those cases and Pinellas County had 116. Travel-associated dengue cases reached 451 in 2026. Travel-associated chikungunya fever cases reached 114, while two locally acquired chikungunya fever cases were reported in Miami-Dade County with onset in August. No locally acquired Zika fever cases were reported this week or in 2026. No travel-associated Oropouche fever or Zika fever cases were reported this week. As of Nov. 14, Bay, Brevard, Broward, Columbia, Leon, Manatee, Martin, Palm Beach, Polk, Sarasota and Walton counties were under a mosquito-borne illness advisory. Alachua, Citrus, Duval, Hillsborough, Holmes, Miami-Dade, Orange, Pasco, Pinellas and Seminole counties were under a mosquito-borne illness alert. No veterinary cases were reported this week. One mosquito pool tested positive for dengue in Pasco County

supplementary_news.content: India Cities Delhi Mumbai Kolkata +5 more World US UK Europe Asia +3 more Entertainment Bollywood South OTT TV +3 more Sports Cricket Hockey Football Pickleball +7 more Business Personal Finance Markets Companies Economy Lifestyle Relationships Health Fashion Books +3 more Videos India World Shows Newshour +5 more More Latest News Education Auto Opinion Viral Viral 26 Nov 2026 | 08:28 AM IST Live TV SIGN IN Latest India World Entertainment Sports Business Lifestyle Opinion Pickleball Tech Videos Viral US-Iran War Live UpdatesUP Election Seat-Sharing HeatStock Market TodayRamayana Box Office CollectionToyota Innova Hycross Facelift Launch TodayDelhi AQI Today Search "Sporting Vs Man Utd" Health Can Mosquitoes Help Fight Dengue Instead Of Spreading It? Authored by: Simran Sukhnani Updated: Nov 25, 2026, 13:01 IST Scientists are using Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes to fight dengue, with Brazil reporting promising results. Here's how this unusual approach works and whether it could help India tackle outbreaks. Can mosquitos help prevent dengue (Credits: iStock) follow usfollow us Scientists have reported a promising breakthrough in the fight against mosquito-borne diseases, and it involves using mosquitoes themselves as a weapon. In Brazil, specially bred mosquitoes carrying a naturally occurring bacterium called Wolbachia were associated with a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections among children exposed to them. The findings have sparked fresh interest in an approach that could change how the world tackles mosquito-borne diseases. The idea sounds unusual - instead of killing mosquitoes, scientists are releasing mosquitoes that are less capable of spreading infections. But how does this work, and could it make a difference in countries like India, where dengue outbreaks remain a recurring public health concern? How Do Wolbachia-Infected Mosquitoes Work? Wolbachia is a naturally occurring bacterium found in several insect species. It is introduced into Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, the primary carriers of dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses. Once established inside the mosquito, the bacterium makes it harder for these viruses to multiply and reach the mosquito's saliva, reducing the likelihood of transmission when it bites a human. The important difference here is that these mosquitoes are not genetically modified to become a different species, nor are they designed to eliminate mosquitoes altogether. The objective is to make the existing mosquito population less capable of transmitting disease. The bacterium also has an interesting way of sustaining itself. Female mosquitoes pass Wolbachia on to their offspring, allowing it to gradually establish itself in local mosquito populations. This means the intervention does not necessarily require repeated releases indefinitely once the bacterium becomes established. What Did The Brazil Study Find? The latest findings come from a four-year study conducted in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, involving more than 5,700 children. Researchers compared neighbourhoods where Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes had been released with similar neighbourhoods that continued to receive conventional mosquito-control interventions. What is the Wolbachia bacterium in mosquitos (Credits: iStock) The study found approximately 69% fewer dengue and chikungunya infections among children in areas where Wolbachia mosquitoes were released. The reduction reportedly persisted even during Brazil's severe dengue outbreak in 2024. Researchers also tested blood samples to identify infections that might otherwise have gone undetected because of mild or unreported symptoms. The findings were presented at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. Could This Approach Work In India? For a country like India, where dengue outbreaks regularly put pressure on healthcare facilities, the possibility of reducing transmission without relying entirely on insecticides is significant. However, experts believe the approach needs to be understood as an additional layer of protection rather than a replacement for existing preventive measures. Dr. Paritosh Baghel, Senior Consultant Physician at S.L. Raheja Hospital, Mumbai, explains the distinction, "As opposed to traditional methods of mosquito control, which emphasise the eradication of the mosquito populations, this method seeks to inhibit the mosquito populations' ability to spread infections." Dr. Umang Agarwal, Consultant, Infectious Diseases at P.D. Hinduja Hospital and MRC, Khar, believes the approach represents an important shift in disease prevention. "The novelty of the approach is in the fact that, contrary to the elimination of mosquitoes, scientists are now looking for ways to reduce their capabilities to spread diseases," he says. However, there are important considerations before such a strategy can be adopted widely. Its effectiveness depends on successfully establishing Wolbachia in local mosquito populations, and results may vary with geography, mosquito populations and climatic conditions. Dr. Baghel also cautions that promising international findings should not be mistaken for a ready-made solution. India would need appropriate evaluation across its own environmental and epidemiological conditions. Meanwhile, the basics of dengue prevention remain unchanged. Removing stagnant water, preventing mosquito breeding, using repellents and wearing protective clothing are still essential. Recognising symptoms such as persistent fever, severe body pain, vomiting and abdominal pain, and seeking timely medical attention can also help prevent complications. The idea of fighting mosquitoes with mosquitoes may sound counterintuitive, but it offers an interesting possibility: perhaps the answer to controlling some mosquito-borne diseases is not eliminating every mosquito, but changing what they are capable of transmitting. A study of more than 5,700 Brazilian children found roughly 69% fewer dengue and chikungunya infections in neighborhoods where Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes were released. The bacteria, harmless to people, reduce mosquitoes’ ability to transmit certain viruses and can spread through offspring, potentially establishing the trait in local populations. The findings arrive as Florida reports more than 650 locally acquired dengue cases. The virus is also on the rise in Southern California. WASHINGTON — Children who lived in Brazilian neighborhoods buzzing with a special kind of mosquito were far less likely to catch dengue or another worrisome virus, chikungunya, new research shows. A major study of more than 5,700 children in one of the world’s dengue hot spots offers new evidence that breeding mosquitoes unable to transmit these viruses can be a viable strategy rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten. In neighborhoods populated by these so-called Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes, researchers found about a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections in schoolchildren compared with similar neighborhoods without them — an effect sustained even during Brazil’s severe 2024 dengue outbreak, said Dr. Sri Edupuganti of Emory University, part of the international research team. Advertisement The researchers reported the findings Saturday at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. “This is really exciting,” said Dr. David Hamer, a global health expert at Boston University who wasn’t involved with the Brazilian study. He predicts that pairing more use of these Wolbachia mosquitoes with existing steps to fight mosquito-borne disease could “knock dengue down to much lower levels” in many places. The latest research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus, what appears to be the biggest in any U.S. state since at least the 1940s. Advertisement Usually in the continental U.S., dengue is found mostly in people who traveled internationally. But as of Friday, Florida health officials had tallied more than 650 locally acquired cases, about three-quarters of them in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa. Mosquito-borne dengue and other viruses have also been on the rise in Southern California. Outside the U.S., the nonprofit World Mosquito Program has pioneered the Wolbachia strategy. How it works: Scientists breed mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia. It is harmless to people and common in many insects, although not dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. The bacteria dramatically reduce the mosquitoes’ ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes spread the bacteria to their offspring, so releasing enough of the specially bred insects — males and females — into an area allows Wolbachia to gradually become established in the local mosquito population. Field trials and other studies in Indonesia and elsewhere have shown the strategy can significantly lower dengue diagnoses. But because people with mild symptoms may not be diagnosed, the new study in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, went further. Researchers tested blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya or the Zika virus. The four-year study compared children living in neighborhoods that all got the same pesticide and other mosquito-control interventions, but half were randomly assigned to have Wolbachia mosquitoes released into the area. There were too few cases of Zika to calculate whether the special mosquitoes had any effect on that disease. Neergaard writes for the Associated Press. supplementary_news.content: Skip to main content YaleNews Videos In the Media Subscribe Explore Topics Search Across Yale: Yale’s Impact on America Healthier Holiday Meals Practicing Gratitude Close Search Search Videos In the Media Subscribe Across Yale: Yale’s Impact on America Healthier Holiday Meals Practicing Gratitude Alumni Arts & Humanities Business Campus & Community Environment Health & Medicine International Law Science & Technology Social Sciences In Memoriam Story Collections Yale College Graduate School of Arts & Sciences School of Architecture School of Art Divinity School David Geffen School of Drama School of Engineering & Applied Science School of the Environment Jackson School of Global Affairs Law School School of Management School of Medicine School of Music School of Nursing School of Public Health Search YaleNews Share Close Share this page Post to Facebook Post to Twitter Post to LinkedIn Email this page Print this page Health & Medicine ‘Wolbachia’ mosquito: The bug that could change everything Yale School of Public Health researchers are investigating how a naturally occurring bacterium can help control dengue, Zika, and other mosquito-borne diseases. Nov 23, 2026 8 min read By Meg Dalton Afeez Sodeinde with mosquitoes in the Vogels Lab. Photo by Kristen Ortega Listen to this story ‘Wolbachia’ mosquito: The bug that could change everything 0:00 / 9:52 In 2015, Albert Ko spent several months in the maternity hospitals of Salvador, a city in Northeast Brazil where he has been working with the Brazilian Ministry of Health since the 1990s. At that time, the city was the epicenter of a Zika epidemic, which eventually spread throughout the Americas and infected roughly 1.5 million people. Ko witnessed firsthand the impact of this mosquito-borne disease on the local population, which caused severe birth defects in infants whose mothers came from the poorest communities in the city and were infected during pregnancy with the Zika virus. “Our team’s work in Brazil centers on this intersection between infectious disease and social justice,” said Ko, the Albert Ko, the Raj and Indra Nooyi Professor of Public Health at the Yale School of Public Health (YSPH). “In Brazil and many countries, social inequity, combined with rapid urbanization, has led to the emergence of diseases, such as Zika, which disproportionally affect marginalized populations living in urban informal settlements.” The Zika epidemic prompted Ko and his team in Brazil and Yale to tackle the question how to prevent diseases transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, including dengue and chikungunya as well as Zika, in these vulnerable communities and beyond. Today, Ko, alongside Chantal Vogels, an assistant professor of epidemiology (microbial diseases) at YSPH, are investigating just that. One in the field and the other in the lab, their research uses Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes as a tool for controlling dengue, Zika, and other mosquito-borne diseases. Wolbachia is a naturally occurring bacterium that resides inside some insects. If you introduce Wolbachia into the Aedes aegypti mosquito, which does not naturally harbor the bacteria, it acts as a vaccine and prevents the transmission of viruses, such the dengue virus, within the mosquito. Wolbachia-infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes being reared at the EVITA trial site in Belo Horizonte Brazil. Photo by Flávio Carvalho As the global climate continues to warm, the work of Ko and Vogels will prove even more critical. More and more communities are seeing upticks in mosquito-borne diseases beyond the tropics, including in the United States. This year, for example, the state of Florida has seen a record number of dengue fever cases, more than 400 so far. In the lab With a background in entomology and virology, Vogels has dedicated her career to studying mosquito and tick-borne viruses. Specifically, she’s focused on understanding the factors that affect transmission and control. “The ultimate goal of my work is to better mitigate the burden of mosquito and tick-borne viruses on public health,” Vogels said. Vogels got interested in studying Wolbachia specifically because it seemed like such a novel method for biological control. She was intrigued by the interplay between viruses like dengue, the Wolbachia bacterium, and mosquitoes. So, she started studying the genetic diversity of viruses and how that variation affects the effectiveness of mosquito control strategies. “I don’t think there’s ever going be a single control intervention,” Vogels said. “You need an integrated approach, and I do think that Wolbachia fits within that toolbox.” Members of Vogels Lab. From left: Chantal Vogels, Julian W. Bakker, Afeez Sodeinde, and Nicole Feriancek. Photo by Kristen Ortega Right now, there are two main strategies that are being used in the field. The first method uses Wolbachia as a form of birth control for the mosquito population. This method relies on mass rearing of large numbers of mosquitoes in the laboratory with Wolbachia which are then released to the wild. Male mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia are not able to produce offspring with the wildtype females. This method suppresses the local mosquito population. “That method relies on continued release of the male mosquitoes,” Vogels said. “When you stop, mosquito populations can reestablish themselves again.” The second method uses Wolbachia as a form of vaccination for mosquitoes. With this method, female Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes are released into the wild. They can have offspring with either Wolbachia-carrying or wildtype males, and because Wolbachia is maternally transmitted, the offspring would also carry Wolbachia in either case. This method replaces the local mosquito population. Initially in the lab, these two methods — suppression and replacement — have been introduced through field trials. In some cases, the results have been good. In other cases, the results have been mixed. That’s where Vogels’s research comes in. In her lab, Vogels and her research team use experimental approaches to understand how Wolbachia can be used to control dengue. They’re able to manipulate different conditions to understand the factors that impact the inhibition that Wolbachia is causing in terms of dengue transmission. “If we know what factors impact control methods like Wolbachia, then we can immediately inform those control interventions and make a big impact in the field,” Vogels said. One of the important factors is the feeding behavior of mosquitoes, or how frequently they have “blood meals,” which refers to the ingestion of blood by female mosquitoes after puncturing the skin of vertebrates. Vogels’s team has found that natural feeding behavior has a reduced effect on Wolbachia in terms of inhibiting dengue. In another study, they looked at how genetic differences in dengue virus impact Wolbachia’s ability to inhibit it. They tested two Wolbachia strains against 60 different dengue virus samples from all four serotypes. They found that both the Wolbachia strains and dengue virus samples varied in how well they worked together, with some pairs inhibiting more effectively than others. Fieldwork As Vogels has been experimenting with these methods in the lab, Ko has been testing them out in the field. He started working in Brazil on Wolbachia interventions in 2017, informed by his experience in mounting the public health response to the Zika epidemic in preceding years. At that time, his friend and fellow researcher, Mauro Teixeira, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, was designing a cluster randomized controlled trial for population replacement, where Wolbachia is used as a form of vaccination for mosquitoes. The duo also worked closely with Luciano Moreira, a senior researcher at the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation, the research branch of the Brazilian Ministry of Health which Ko has been affiliated with for the last 30 years. The EVITA trial team, which includes Mauro Teixeira (eighth from left) from the Federal University of Minas Gerais, Sri Edupuganti (ninth front from left) from Emory University, Derek Cummings (tenth back from left) from Johns Hopkins University, and Albert Ko (third from right), and YSPH doctoral student Elisabeth Nelson (fourth back from left). Paloma Carcamo, another YSPH doctoral student, was not present. Credit: Luciano Moreira and Flávio Carvalho The trial, called EVITA, launched in 2020 with funding support from the National Institutes of Health and Brazilian Ministry of Health. Their approach involved replacing the native mosquito population with Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes, which are resistant to dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses. With this approach, researchers only have to release the mosquitoes once, rather than continuously releasing infected male mosquitoes to suppress mosquito populations, which can be costly and challenging to do in resource-poor settings, particularly in the Global South. For the trial, the EVITA team designated 58 clusters, or neighborhoods surrounding primary schools within the city of Belo Horizonte, which is home to 3 million people. Moreira and his team grew colonies of Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes, and by car and motorcycle, released them in half of the neighborhoods. In total, 32 million mosquitoes were released during the trial. Teixeira and his team then followed the school children living in both the neighborhoods that received the intervention and those that did not to evaluate whether they had a dengue or chikungunya infection. EVITA team implementing patient enrollment and protocol in neighborhoods at the trial’s start during the pandemic in 2020. Credit: Luciano Moreira and Flávio Carvalho “The primary outcome was to determine the effectiveness of preventing infection with dengue or chikungunya in schoolchildren living in neighborhoods where Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes were released,” said Ko, who is also a professor of medicine (infectious diseases) at Yale School of Medicine. After the conclusion of the EVITA trial, in 2024, an international team of investigators — including Teixeira, Moreira, Ko, and YSPH doctoral students, Elisabeth Nelson and Paloma Carcamo — spent the past two years analyzing the findings. The findings — which were presented at the meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene on Nov. 21, 2026 — showed that the intervention worked; it reduced the risk of infection with dengue by 69% and infection with chikungunya by 73%. Perhaps more impressive, researchers say, the Wolbachia population replacement prevented infections during the largest epidemic of dengue in recorded history in Brazil, which occurred in the trial’s last year in 2024. “The 2024 epidemic was a pressure test that demonstrated that Wolbachia population replacement protected communities even under conditions of intense transmission,” Ko said. They also demonstrated that the intervention not only prevented dengue and chikungunya infections among school children but also significantly reduced the number cases of dengue and chikungunya in all age groups who sought medical care at health posts or were hospitalized. “The EVITA trial is an important step forward in the search for sustainable, scalable approaches to protecting people from dengue, chikungunya and Zika,” Ko said. “Over 4 billion of the world’s population live in regions, including parts of the U.S., where diseases transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito occur and this number will increase because of future trends in climate change and urbanization.” Health & Medicine Solutions How to prepare youth to respond to firearm injury risk Nov 25, 2026 4 min read Discoveries Can a common blood thinner stop osteoarthritis? supplementary_news.content: News Around the World Brazil study links Wolbachia bacterium to 69% reduction in infections — The Independent UA.NEWS 21 November 2026 17:31 A study in the Brazilian city of Belo Horizonte involving more than 5,700 children found an approximately 69% lower incidence of dengue and chikungunya infections in areas with mosquitoes carrying the Wolbachia bacterium than in similar areas. As The Independent reports , this effect persisted even during a severe dengue outbreak in Brazil in 2024. The results were reported by Dr. Shri Edupuganti of Emory University, who was part of the international research team. The findings were presented at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. How Wolbachia works Scientists breed mosquitoes that carry Wolbachia, a bacterium common among many insects and harmless to humans. Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which can transmit dengue, do not usually carry this bacterium. Wolbachia significantly reduces mosquitoes’ ability to transmit certain viruses. Females pass the bacterium on to their offspring. Therefore, after a sufficient number of such mosquitoes — males and females — are released, Wolbachia can gradually become established in the local population. Field trials in Indonesia and other countries have already shown that this strategy can noticeably reduce the number of diagnosed dengue cases. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Blood tests of participants In Belo Horizonte, researchers did not limit themselves to data on confirmed diagnoses, since people with mild symptoms may not receive such a diagnosis. They analyzed participants’ blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya, or the Zika virus. Boston University global health expert David Hamer, who was not involved in the study, called the results encouraging. In his view, combining this approach with other measures to combat mosquito-borne diseases could substantially reduce the spread of dengue. The study was presented amid a major dengue outbreak in the U.S. state of Florida. As of Friday, state officials had recorded more than 650 cases of local transmission, about three quarters of them in Hillsborough County, where Tampa is located. Read us on Download our app
